title: Prevalence and genotype distribution of norovirus and rotavirus among children under five with diarrheal infection in lower-middle-income countries after Rotavirus vaccine introduction: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Rotavirus and norovirus are the leading viral causes of acute diarrheal disease worldwide. Both viruses encompass multiple genotypes and subgenotypes, and this genetic diversity presents a significant challenge to rotavirus vaccine effectiveness and development. High-quality evidence on the prevalence and circulating genotypes of these enteric viruses among children under five years of age remains limited, particularly following the introduction of rotavirus vaccination in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesizes available evidence on the prevalence and genotype distribution of norovirus and rotavirus in this population. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted across five major databases PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Embase, and Web of Science between February 20 and 28, 2026. Duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, full-text review and data extraction were performed independently by two investigators using the Rayyan web-based platform. STATA version 17 software was used for statistical analysis. A random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled prevalence and effect sizes. Heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q statistic, the I 2 statistic, forest plots, and Galbraith plots. Publication bias was assessed using both graphical (funnel plots) and statistical methods. Results A total of 35,704 children under five years with diarrheal infection from LMICs were included across eligible studies. The overall pooled prevalence of norovirus and rotavirus combined was 18% (95% CI: 15–21%). Rotavirus had a higher pooled prevalence than norovirus, at 24% (95% CI: 19.6–28.3%) and 13% (95% CI: 11–15%), respectively. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I 2 = 98.72%, p Conclusions Norovirus and rotavirus remain significant causes of diarrheal disease among children under five in LMICs, even after the introduction of rotavirus vaccination. Approximately one in five children with diarrheal illness were infected with at least one of these virusesGII, particularly subgenotype GII.4, was the dominant norovirus strain, while G3[P8] and G1[P8] were the most prevalent rotavirus genotypes. These findings underscore the need to strengthen surveillance systems, consider circulating genotypes in vaccine formulation, and continuously monitor genotype shifts within the population.

Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I 2 = 98.72%, p Conclusions Norovirus and rotavirus remain significant causes of diarrheal disease among children under five in LMICs, even after the introduction of rotavirus vaccination. Approximately one in five children with diarrheal illness were infected with at least one of these virusesGII, particularly subgenotype GII.4, was the dominant norovirus strain, while G3[P8] and G1[P8] were the most prevalent rotavirus genotypes. title: Molecular Prevalence and Determinants of Adenovirus and Norovirus Among Diarrhoeic Children in Ilorin Metropolis, Kwara State, Nigeria
abstract: Viral gastroenteritis remains a major public health concern and a leading cause of morbidity among children under five worldwide. Adenovirus (Adv) and Norovirus (Nv) are important etiological agents, yet data on their prevalence and determinants in North-central Nigeria are limited. A cross-sectional study involving 100 children under 5 years with acute diarrhoea was conducted at the Children’s Specialist Hospital, Ilorin, Kwara State between February to December, 2024. Virus detection was performed using qPCR, while a semi-structured questionnaire collected sociodemographic and environmental data. Associations were analyzed using chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression. Adenovirus prevalence was high (71%), while Norovirus GI and GII were detected in 4% and 12% of cases, respectively. Coinfection of Adv and Nv occurred in 13% of participants. Adenovirus infection was significantly associated with sociodemographic and sanitation factors whereas no significant predictors were identified for Norovirus. Multivariable analysis showed sanitation-related factors as the strongest predictors. Toilets located near water sources increased the risk of infection, whereas open defecation had lower odds than water closet use. Both infections were more prevalent during the wet season. These findings highlight key determinants of Adv and Nv infections in children under five, underscoring the need for targeted public health interventions among vulnerable populations.

title: Editorial: Plant and human pathogen interactions: gaining insights into the impact of environmental and crop management factors, volume II
abstract: Promoting increased consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables remains a cornerstone of global public health strategies aimed at preventing noncommunicable diseases and addressing micronutrient deficiencies. However, the safety of fresh produce continues to be challenged by contamination with human enteric pathogens. The persistence and dissemination of human pathogens within agricultural ecosystems represent a complex interplay between microbial physiology, plant-associated niches, environmental stressors, and crop management practices. Following the insights gathered in Volume I of this Research Topic, Volume II brings together four contributions that advance our understanding of these dynamics. Together, these studies reveal how biological adaptation, produce surface characteristics, and environmental reservoirs influence the persistence, transmission, and control of human pathogens and antimicrobial resistance within agricultural systems.A foundational element of pathogen persistence is the ability of human enteric bacteria to adapt to non-host, plant-associated environments. In their comprehensive review, Han et al. (2025) synthesize the metabolic adaptations utilized by Salmonella enterica to survive and colonize plant tissues and agricultural substrates. The authors delineate how S. enterica dynamically reprograms its central carbon and nitrogen metabolism in response to nutrients available in root exudates, leaf apoplastic fluids, and plant tissues. enterica prioritizes glucose metabolism through glycolysis, shifts to gluconeogenesis under sugar-limiting conditions, and exploits alternative carbon sources such as glycerol, fatty acids, and organic acids. Furthermore, de novo amino acid biosynthesis, particularly cysteine via sulfate assimilation, emerges as an indispensable metabolic hub required for bacterial fitness across diverse plant hosts and stress conditions. By highlighting this metabolic plasticity, Han et al. (2025) provide insights into how human pathogens exploit plant metabolic niches, identifying physiological vulnerabilities that could be targeted to prevent preharvest colonization.Interactions at the plant surface are relevant for pathogen attachment, retention, and susceptibility to post-harvest sanitation. Addressing this physical interface, Lightbown and DiCaprio (2025) investigated the impact of leafy green microscale surface topography on the recovery and chemical sanitizer inactivation of Tulane virus (TV), a surrogate for human norovirus. Comparing fresh romaine lettuce and spinach leaves across growth stages and leaf axes, the authors demonstrated that spinach leaf maturity significantly influences chemical inactivation: younger leaves allowed higher viral inactivation by sodium hypochlorite than older leaves. Crucially, the authors engineered polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) topomimetic artificial leaf surfaces ("replicasts") to decouple physical structural attributes from biological variability. By modulating replicast hydrophobicity with lowconcentration surfactants, the artificial surfaces faithfully reproduced viral recovery trends observed on fresh plant tissue, validating topomimetic replicasts as standardized physical tools for produce safety research.Expanding this physical engineering framework to soft fruits, Lightbown and DiCaprio (2026) evaluated PDMS topomimetic artificial surfaces modeled after blueberries, strawberries, and raspberries. Soft berries present intricate surface features, ranging from smooth epicuticular wax on blueberries to achene pits on strawberries and dense trichomes on raspberry drupelets, that create micro-refuges protecting viruses from post-harvest wash treatments. Their findings demonstrated that berry type markedly dictates viral retention, with raspberries retaining higher viral titers than blueberries or strawberries. Surface replicasts of all three berry types closely mirrored the recovery levels obtained from fresh fruits, confirming that physical micro-architecture is a primary driver of viral adhesion and protection against sanitizer wash solutions. These data indicate that while berry replicasts may have utility in modeling surface adhesion of viruses to berries and in viral recovery studies, they are not suitable for studies of viral inactivation by chemical sanitizers.Beyond pathogen persistence and sanitizer efficacy, agricultural environments are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), introducing an additional dimension to produce safety risk assessment. (2025) conducted whole-genome sequencing on 87 multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial strains isolated from leafy greens, root zone soil, and bulk soil within urban agriculture systems. Representing 14 genera dominated by Pseudomonas, Serratia, Providencia, and Bacillus, these environmental isolates exhibited extensive resistomes primarily encoding multidrug efflux systems, β-lactamases, and tetracycline resistance determinants. All MDR isolates harbored mobile genetic elements (MGEs), with multiple antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) located in close physical proximity (<5 kb) to transposons, plasmids, or prophages. These findings support the notion that urban agricultural soils and fresh produce can act as environmental reservoirs and potential mobilization vectors for AMR elements, emphasizing the necessity of monitoring resistome dynamics alongside conventional foodborne pathogens.Overall, these studies demonstrate that both biological adaptation and environmental context shape the persistence, transmission, and control of food safety hazards in agricultural systems. Importantly, these findings also underscore how crop-management decisions may influence foodsafety risks across production systems. Deciphering bacterial metabolic flexibility, standardizing physical produce surface models for viral wash treatments, and mapping environmental resistomes in urban agroecosystems collectively inform risk assessment, agronomic policy, and post-harvest intervention protocols. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on human noroviruses and their role in human disease, particularly examining how environmental and crop management factors influence the persistence, transmission, and control of these pathogens within agricultural ecosystems. The central question is how these factors affect the behavior of human noroviruses and their potential to cause gastroenteritis.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a collection of four contributions that analyze the interactions between human pathogens and agricultural systems. The evidence includes studies on metabolic adaptations of Salmonella enterica, surface topography of leafy greens and berries, and the presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in urban agricultural environments. The review does not explicitly report a meta-analysis or pooled estimate but synthesizes findings from these studies.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the persistence and transmission of human pathogens, including noroviruses, are influenced by both biological adaptation and environmental factors. It highlights the importance of understanding how produce surface characteristics and environmental reservoirs affect pathogen survival and the need for targeted interventions in food safety.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies gaps in understanding how specific crop management practices influence norovirus persistence and transmission. It also notes that while the studies provide insights into the role of environmental factors, there is limited data on the direct impact of norovirus genogroups or variants on these dynamics. Additionally, the review acknowledges the need for further research on the role of physical surface structures in viral inactivation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should focus on deciphering the metabolic flexibility of human pathogens, standardizing physical models of produce surfaces for viral wash treatments, and mapping environmental resistomes in urban agroecosystems. These efforts could inform more effective risk assessment strategies, agronomic policies, and post-harvest intervention protocols.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the interactions between human noroviruses and agricultural ecosystems, emphasizing how environmental and crop management factors influence pathogen persistence, transmission, and control. It highlights the role of produce surface characteristics and microbial adaptation in shaping food safety risks. The review underscores the need for targeted interventions that address both biological and ecological mechanisms underlying pathogen survival. While the studies provide insights into the behavior of human pathogens, they also identify gaps in understanding the specific impact of norovirus genogroups and the effectiveness of chemical sanitizers against these viruses. The findings suggest that future research should focus on standardizing physical models of produce surfaces and monitoring environmental resistomes to improve food safety strategies.

elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述汇集了四篇文章,分析了人类病原体与农业系统之间的相互作用。证据包括对肠道沙门氏菌代谢适应、绿叶蔬菜和浆果表面形貌以及城市农业环境中抗菌素耐药性 (AMR) 存在的研究。该综述没有明确报告荟萃分析或汇总估计,而是综合了这些研究的结果。

elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议,未来的研究应侧重于破译人类病原体的代谢灵活性、标准化病毒清洗 治疗 的农产品表面物理模型,以及绘制城市农业生态系统中的环境抗性组图。这些努力可以为更有效的风险评估策略、农艺政策和收获后干预方案提供信息。

Surface replicasts of all three berry types closely mirrored the recovery levels obtained from fresh fruits, confirming that physical micro-architecture is a primary driver of viral adhesion and protection against sanitizer wash solutions. These data indicate that while berry replicasts may have utility in modeling surface adhesion of viruses to berries and in viral recovery studies, they are not suitable for studies of viral inactivation by chemical sanitizers.Beyond pathogen persistence and sanitizer efficacy, agricultural environments are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), introducing an additional dimension to produce safety risk assessment. (2025) conducted whole-genome sequencing on 87 multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial strains isolated from leafy greens, root zone soil, and bulk soil within urban agriculture systems. Representing 14 genera dominated by Pseudomonas, Serratia, Providencia, and Bacillus, these environmental isolates exhibited extensive resistomes primarily encoding multidrug efflux systems, β-lactamases, and tetracycline resistance determinants. All MDR isolates harbored mobile genetic elements (MGEs), with multiple antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) located in close physical proximity (<5 kb) to transposons, plasmids, or prophages. These findings support the notion that urban agricultural soils and fresh produce can act as environmental reservoirs and potential mobilization vectors for AMR elements, emphasizing the necessity of monitoring resistome dynamics alongside conventional foodborne pathogens.Overall, these studies demonstrate that both biological adaptation and environmental context shape the persistence, transmission, and control of food safety hazards in agricultural systems. Importantly, these findings also underscore how crop-management decisions may influence foodsafety risks across production systems. Deciphering bacterial metabolic flexibility, standardizing physical produce surface models for viral wash treatments, and mapping environmental resistomes in urban agroecosystems collectively inform risk assessment, agronomic policy, and post-harvest intervention protocols. (2025) highlight the remarkable metabolic adaptability of S. enterica to plant-associated environments, suggesting that differences in plant genotypes and their associated nutrient profiles may influence pathogen colonization potential. Lightbown andDiCaprio (2025, 2026) demonstrate that harvest maturity, produce type, and post-harvest washing practices affect viral retention and sanitizer efficacy through differences in surface architecture. Likewise, Harrelson et al. (2025) show that urban agricultural soils and produce can serve as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance, emphasizing the importance of understanding how management practices, including irrigation and soil amendment strategies, influence the composition and dissemination of resistance determinants. Together, these management factors interact with environmental conditions, including moisture, temperature, soil properties, and plant developmental stage, to shape persistence and transmission within agricultural ecosystems. This improved understanding of how enteric pathogens interact with fruit and vegetable production systems moves the field beyond solely exclusionary approaches to food safety and supports the development of more targeted interventions that address the biological and ecological mechanisms underlying pathogen survival. Continued research at the intersection of plant biology, microbiology, and agricultural systems remains essential to advance the safe and sustainable production of fresh fruits and vegetables globally.
abstract_zh: 促进增加新鲜水果和蔬菜的消费仍然是旨在预防非传染性疾病和解决微量营养素缺乏的全球公共卫生战略的基石。然而,新鲜农产品的安全性继续受到人类肠道病原体污染的挑战。人类病原体在农业生态系统中的持续存在和传播代表了微生物生理学、植物相关生态位、环境压力源和作物管理实践之间复杂的相互作用。继本研究主题第一卷中收集的见解之后,第二卷汇集了四项贡献,以增进我们对这些动态的理解。这些研究共同揭示了生物适应、农产品表面特征和环境 储存宿主 如何影响农业系统中人类病原体的持久性、传播 以及对人类病原体和抗菌素耐药性的控制。病原体持久性的一个基本要素是人类肠道细菌适应非 宿主、植物相关环境的能力。在他们的综合评论中,Han 等人。(2025) 合成了肠沙门氏菌用于生存和定植植物组织和农业基质的代谢适应性。作者描述了肠沙门氏菌如何动态地重新编程其中心碳和氮代谢,以响应根分泌物、叶质外体液和植物组织中可用的营养物质。Enterica 优先通过糖酵解进行葡萄糖代谢,在糖限制条件下转向糖异生,并利用甘油、脂肪酸和有机酸等替代碳源。此外,从头氨基酸生物合成,特别是通过硫酸盐同化的半胱氨酸,成为细菌适应不同植物 宿主 和胁迫条件所需的不可或缺的代谢中心。通过强调这种代谢可塑性,Han 等人。(2025) 提供了关于人类病原体如何利用植物代谢生态位的见解,确定了可以预防收获前定殖的生理脆弱性。植物表面的相互作用与病原体的附着、保留和对收获后卫生的敏感性相关。针对这一物理界面,Lightbown 和 DiCaprio (2025) 研究了绿叶微型表面形貌对杜兰病毒 (TV)(人类 诺如病毒 的替代品)恢复和化学消毒剂灭活的影响。作者通过比较新鲜的生菜和菠菜叶子的生长阶段和叶轴,发现菠菜叶子的成熟度显着影响化学灭活:较老的叶子相比,较老的叶子更容易被次氯酸钠灭活。至关重要的是,作者设计了聚二甲基硅氧烷(PDMS)拓扑模拟人造叶子表面(“复制品”),以将物理结构属性与生物变异性分开。通过用低浓度表面活性剂调节复制体的疏水性,人造表面忠实地再现了在新鲜植物组织上观察到的病毒恢复趋势,验证了拓扑模拟复制体作为生产安全研究的标准化物理工具。将这种物理工程框架扩展到软水果,Lightbown 和 DiCaprio (2026) 评估了以蓝莓、草莓和覆盆子为模型的 PDMS 拓扑模拟人造表面。柔软的浆果呈现出复杂的表面特征,从蓝莓上光滑的表皮蜡到草莓上的瘦果核,再到覆盆子核果上密集的毛状体,这些特征形成了微避难所,保护病毒免受采后清洗 治疗 的侵害。他们的研究结果表明,浆果类型显着决定了病毒的保留,覆盆子比蓝莓或草莓保留了更高的病毒滴度。所有三种浆果类型的表面复制品都密切反映了从新鲜水果中获得的恢复水平,证实物理微结构是病毒粘附和针对消毒剂清洗溶液的保护的主要驱动因素。这些数据表明,虽然浆果复制体可能有助于模拟病毒对浆果的表面粘附和病毒回收研究,但它们不适合研究化学消毒剂对病毒的灭活。除了病原体持久性和消毒剂功效之外,农业环境越来越被认为是抗菌素耐药性(AMR)的储存宿主,引入了额外的维度来进行安全风险评估。(2025) 对从城市农业系统内的绿叶蔬菜、根区土壤和大块土壤中分离出的 87 种多重耐药 (MDR) 细菌菌株进行了全 基因组 测序。这些环境分离株代表以假单胞菌属、沙雷氏菌属、普罗维登斯氏菌属和芽孢杆菌属为主的 14 个属,表现出广泛的耐药组,主要编码多药外排系统、β-内酰胺酶和四环素耐药决定簇。所有 MDR 分离株都含有可移动遗传元件 (MGE),其中多个抗生素抗性基因 (ARG) 与转座子、质粒或前噬菌体物理位置非常接近 (<5 kb)。这些发现支持这样的观点,即城市农业土壤和新鲜农产品可以充当环境储存宿主和AMR元素的潜在动员媒介,强调了与传统食源性病原体一起监测抗药性动态的必要性。总体而言,这些研究表明,生物适应和环境背景塑造了农业系统中食品安全危害的持久性、媒介和控制。重要的是,这些发现还强调了作物管理决策如何影响整个生产系统的食品安全风险。破译细菌代谢灵活性、标准化病毒清洗 治疗 的物理产品表面模型以及绘制城市农业生态系统中的环境抗性组图,共同为风险评估、农艺政策和收获后干预方案提供信息。(2025) 强调了肠沙门氏菌对植物相关环境的显着代谢适应性,表明植物基因型及其相关营养成分的差异可能会影响病原体定植潜力。Lightbown 和 DiCaprio(2025、2026)证明,收获成熟度、农产品类型和收获后清洗做法通过表面结构的差异影响病毒保留和消毒剂功效。同样,哈里森等人。(2025)表明城市农业土壤和农产品可以作为抗菌素耐药性的储存宿主,强调了解管理实践(包括灌溉和土壤改良策略)如何影响耐药性决定因素的组成和传播的重要性。这些管理因素与环境条件(包括湿度、温度、土壤性质和植物发育阶段)相互作用,从而形成农业生态系统中的持久性和传播。对肠道病原体如何与水果和蔬菜生产系统相互作用的认识的提高,使该领域超越了食品安全的单一排除方法,并支持开发更有针对性的干预措施,以解决病原体生存的生物和生态机制。植物生物学、微生物学和农业系统交叉领域的持续研究对于促进全球新鲜水果和蔬菜的安全和可持续生产仍然至关重要。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 该综述重点关注人类 诺如病毒 及其在人类疾病中的作用,特别研究环境和作物管理因素如何影响农业生态系统中这些病原体的持久性、传播 和控制。核心问题是这些因素如何影响人类 诺如病毒 的行为及其引起胃肠炎的可能性。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述汇集了四篇文章,分析了人类病原体与农业系统之间的相互作用。证据包括对肠道沙门氏菌代谢适应、绿叶蔬菜和浆果表面形貌以及城市农业环境中抗菌素耐药性 (AMR) 存在的研究。该综述没有明确报告荟萃分析或汇总估计,而是综合了这些研究的结果。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述的结论是,包括诺如病毒在内的人类病原体的持久性和传播受到生物适应和环境因素的影响。它强调了了解农产品表面特性和环境 储存宿主 如何影响病原体生存的重要性以及对食品安全进行有针对性的干预措施的必要性。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该审查确定了在理解特定作物管理实践如何影响 诺如病毒 持久性和 传播 方面的差距。它还指出,虽然这些研究提供了对环境因素作用的见解,但有关 诺如病毒 基因组或变异对这些动态的直接影响的数据有限。此外,该评论承认需要进一步研究物理表面结构在病毒灭活中的作用。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议,未来的研究应侧重于破译人类病原体的代谢灵活性、标准化病毒清洗 治疗 的农产品表面物理模型,以及绘制城市农业生态系统中的环境抗性组图。这些努力可以为更有效的风险评估策略、农艺政策和收获后干预方案提供信息。

full_text: AbstractHuman norovirus GII (HuNoV GII) causes millions of gastrointestinal infections annually and persists for days to weeks in marine waters after wastewater discharge, raising transmission concerns in polluted coastal regions such as the San Diego–Tijuana border between the US and Mexico. We conducted a six-month ddPCR-based monitoring campaign in the Tijuana River Estuary and adjacent coastal ocean to quantify HuNoV GII’s spatial and temporal distribution. This is one of the first such spatially and temporally resolved studies in a coastal marine environment. Mean concentrations were ∼102 copies L–1, reaching > 105 copies L–1 near the mouth of the Tijuana River. HuNoV GII declined with increasing distance from shore and the pollution source, varying across gradients in shoreline proximity, river-mouth distance, alongshore wave-driven surfzone velocity, and river discharge. Concentrations correlated strongly with the widely used fecal indicator Enterococcus (ρ = 0.768), pointing to a shared wastewater source for both. Mean concentration-based swimmer illness risk ranged from 200–350 per 1000 swimmers, far exceeding the EPA benchmark of 32. These findings establish HuNoV GII as a persistent, spatially structured contaminant in this transboundary system and provide a baseline for tracking wastewater infrastructure improvements and informing pathogen risk forecasting models under development.Keywords: environmental pathogens, sewage contamination, gastrointestinal illness, human norovirus, public health Materials and MethodsSite DescriptionThe San Diego–Tijuana border region is located along the west coast of North America at the US–Mexico border. This area spans highly populated cities, the Tijuana River system, and an estuary that connects to the Pacific Ocean just north of the US–Mexico border. This study focuses on sampling conducted along a ∼12 km stretch of the US side of the coastal ocean border region from 19 June 2024 through 30 December 2024.Wastewater from Tijuana is collected by the South Bay International Wastewater Treatment Plant (SBIWTP), operated by the International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC) at the US–Mexico border. If the infrastructure is functional and the flow rate is lower than the treatment plant’s capacity, the water is treated and sent offshore in a pipe to be discharged at the 30 m isobath. However, if there is an infrastructure failure or if flow rates exceed the treatment plant’s capacityfor example, during periods of high rainfall and runoffthe wastewater is released directly into the Tijuana River. It is then carried downstream across the border, into the Tijuana Estuary, and eventually makes its way to the coastal ocean. The IBWC flow gauge directly measures the amount of water that is not being treated and is being discharged into the river; we report this as the river discharge variable in this study. This water is a mixture of raw wastewater and runoff. Thus, the concentration of wastewater can vary with the total discharged amount.Intermittent sources of wastewater enter the lower reaches of the Tijuana River through canyons and collectors, principally Goat Canyon and Smuggler’s Gulch. These channels are not continuously gauged, and the discharges are event-driven (often following rainfall or following infrastructure failures). These sources are considered to be a minor component of the Tijuana River discharge, though they can carry a high concentration of untreated sewage.The San Antonio de Los Buenos (SAB) treatment plant, located ∼10 km south of the US–Mexico border near Punta Bandera, represents another major discharge site. At this location, partially or inadequately treated wastewater is discharged directly onto the beach due to the outfall from SAB. Wastewater from Punta Bandera frequently impacts the study region and represents a significant secondary source of contamination. While there have been some improvements to this treatment facility since our study concluded, the SAB plant is distinct from the SBIWTP at the border and represents an independent wastewater loading pathway to the study area.Site names in this study follow San Diego County monitoring conventions. The prefix “PP” denotes the Playa Punta/Border Fence area adjacent to the river mouth; “IB” denotes Imperial Beach; and “EH” denotes Enhanced Hazard stations maintained by San Diego County. Numeric suffixes indicate cross-shore position: no suffix indicates a shoreline or beach sample, “_1′′ indicates a nearshore station, and “_2′′ indicates an offshore station. Each week, 8 to 12 samples were collected, with occasional gaps due to weather holds on boating or other logistical constraints. An additional four samples were provided by the San Diego County Beach and Bay program every week (EH-030, EH-010, IB-050, and IB-060). In total, 283 samples were collected (∼14–23 at each sampling station), all typically in the morning (0700–1100) to maintain consistency across sampling dates and to ensure samples could be processed within 4 h of collection. In all cases, a sterile, acid-washed 1 L plastic bottle was rinsed three times with collection water before being filled. The bottle was immediately placed on ice for transport to the lab (within 4 h). Processing began immediately on arrival at the lab.1(a) Regional map showing the study region (boxed in red) along the San Diego–Tijuana border. Bathymetry is shown as filled contours, ranging from 0 to 50 m water depth. The pink box outlines the zoom-in shown in panel c. This step produced two fractions for each sample, referred to as the eluent (eluted off the filter) and the filtrate (what passed through the filter). Both fractions were processed independently, and the results were added to give a total HuNoV concentration for each water sample (copies L–1). The volume processed varied from sample to sample because the concentrating pipet automatically stops when the flow becomes restricted. The volume of each sample was determined with a graduated cylinder, and the actual HuNoV concentration was scaled to this initial sampling volume. Processed sample volumes ranged from 71–1000 mL (mean = 871 mL, SD = 144.2 mL).EluentParticles were eluted from the filter using FluidPrep tris elution buffer (Innovaprep HC08001). Elution volume varied but was typically 0.5–2 mL. The eluent was concentrated with an Amicon Ultra 50 kDa MWCO centrifugal filter (Millipore) to a final volume of 20–100 μL. 346.5 μL of Applied Biosystems MagMAX Microbiome Lysis Solution and 3.5 μL of biotechnology grade 2-mercaptoethanol (BME) were added directly to the concentrate, and the resulting mixture was stored at −80 °C until extraction. Extraction typically took place within two weeks of sampling.FiltrateThe filtrate underwent an initial concentration using a Vivaflow 200 50 kDa PES tangential flow filtration (TFF) cassette (Sartorius). This reduced the volume to 7–8 mL, which was further concentrated with Amicon Ultra 50 kDa centrifugal filters to a final volume of 20–100 μL. We then added 346.5 μL of Fisher MagMax Microbiome Ultra lysis buffer and 3.5 μL of BME to the concentrate, and the resulting mixture was stored at −80 °C until extraction. Extraction was carried out at the same time as for the eluent.Recovery efficiency was evaluated for both the filtrate and eluent fractions. A buffer exchange was performed with PBS and an Amicon Ultra 50 kDa centrifugal filter, a dilution series was prepared in molecular grade water, and quantified via RT-ddPCR with the primers of Graziano et al. (Table ). Nucleic acids were extracted with the MagMax Microbiome Ultra kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a KingFisher Flex (Thermo Fisher Scientific) bead handling robot utilizing a custom protocol for the KingFisher. For samples prior to 22 October 2024, 80 U of RNaseOUT was added directly to the final eluent. For all other samples, 50 U of RNaseOUT (Invitrogen) was added to the elution buffer at the start of the KingFisher run. Extracted samples were stored at −80 °C until ddPCR.ddPCRddPCR was carried out approximately every two weeks using an AutoDG droplet generator, PTC Tempo Deepwell thermal cycler, and a QX200 droplet reader (Bio-Rad). full_text_sections.results: ResultsFrom June to December 2024, average HuNoV concentrations varied across several orders of magnitude between the sampling locations (Figure ). Most stations had between 14 and 23 independent weekly measurements. Across 283 total samples, the greatest average concentrations exceeded 105 copies L–1 at the shoreline location closest to the river mouth (PP-010). All other shoreline locations had mean values of approximately 104 copies L–1 and were within 1 order of magnitude of each other, whereas most offshore locations had average values ranging from 102–103 copies L–1. In general, the largest proportion of HuNoV GII for each sample was found in the elution fraction (indicated in pink, Figure S1), with the only exception being an offshore location north of Imperial Beach, where concentrations were generally low.Mean sample recovery determined from the evaluation of the MuNoV spike was 23.8 ± 5.3% with no significant difference between samples collected at the river mouth and Silver Strand State Park Campground according to Welch’s two-sample t test (p = 0.985). Inhibition of RT-ddPCR was generally low, with only beach (including river mouth) samples significantly different from the nuclease-free water control in the eluent fraction according to Kruskal–Wallis with a pairwise Dunn test (p = 0.012), and no significant differences for the filtrate fraction (Figures S2 and S3). The mean counts for the eluent fraction of the beach samples were 70.6% of those observed for the control (SD = 14.7%). The estimated inhibition and loss during recovery are small relative to the observed abundance patterns and consistent with previous studies. Counts from the GMM-based procedure for determining positive droplets were highly correlated to counts from Bio-Rad QuantaSoft (eluant: R 2 = 1.00, filtrate R 2 = 0.98 across all samples, Figures S4 and S5).Clear tendencies toward higher HuNoV concentrations near the river source and shoreline emerged when data were grouped within the broad spatial categories of river mouth, beach, nearshore, and offshore (Figure ; Table notes stations by category). Median concentrations were highest at the river mouth (PP-020) and tended to decrease both northward and southward along the shoreline (Figure a). Similarly, median concentrations tended to decrease with the cross-shore distance (Figure b). Statistical analysis of these trends required a per-sample analysis of the LoB.2Norovirus (HuNoV) concentrations (log10 copies L–1) decrease with (a) distance from the river source and (b) distance from the shoreline. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionAs a pathogen of global concern, there have been several studies on the spatiotemporal distributions of HuNoV in water sources such as lakes, rivers, groundwater, and estuaries. However, measurements in coastal marine environments are limited, with only a handful of studies that describe HuNoV distributions. Some examples include the prevalence of HuNoV in the coastal waters of South Korea or in size-partitioned planktonic communities within the Wassaw and Sapelo Sounds, USA. HuNoV may persist in coastal environments for weeks, as detected for example within Sydney rock oysters, and has been observed up to 7 km away from small craft harbors. For the San Diego region, a previous study has reported HuNoV contamination associated with stormwater discharge at the San Diego River and Tourmaline Creek. The spatial patterns in the HuNoV GII concentration observed in this study are consistent with expectations from coastal transport physics. Our results indicated that HuNoV was widespread over the sampling grid (Figures and S2) and that concentrations were highest at the shoreline and at the river source, decreasing with both cross-shore and along-shore distance (Figures and S2). These spatial gradients agree with expectations and the results from physical models, which have predicted that wastewater discharge from the Tijuana River and further south at the SAB treatment plant at Punta Bandera, Mexico, tends to follow the shoreline, resulting in strong alongshore and cross-shore gradients, as the highly concentrated point sources mix with uncontaminated coastal waters. , The temporal patterns in measured HuNoV concentrations exhibited high temporal variability, often with concentrations measured above 104 copies L–1 followed by periods with low concentration (Figure ). Some of the broad temporal variability over this periodhigh in July-August, low in September-October, increasing again toward the end of November and much of Decemberis likely related to rapid changes in river output driven by wastewater pump diversions in the Tijuana River drainage (Figure a, Table S2). Specifically, a pump diversion in mid-September 2024 drastically decreased Tijuana River flows, and subsequent HuNoV GII concentrations were low or beneath the LoB across most of the region. Similarly, increasing flows later in the year, along with seasonality in HuNoV infections, including a record-breaking spike in community infections toward the end of December 2024 (https://www.cdc.gov/norovirus/php/reporting/norostat-data.html), might have explained the rise in measured HuNoV GII concentrations over the end of the sampling period (Figure ).When tested with a GAM, we found that both mean river discharge rates (a proxy for the amount of sewage entering the ocean from the Tijuana River Estuary) and the alongshore wave-driven velocity estimated near Imperial Beach (which drives alongshore transport inside the surfzone) could help explain up to 40% of the deviance in the HuNoV GII measurements (Table ). While not meant for predictive applications, the GAM results imply that there is a combination of additional factors that influences HuNoV distributions in this region. These factors could include the wastewater fraction discharged further south in Mexican waters at Punta Bandera, the variable HuNoV disease and epidemiological trends in Tijuana, the relative abundance of different strains of HuNoV not analyzed in this study (e.g., GI or GIV), and the biological stability and settling rates of HuNoV in a range of coastal conditions (e.g., temperature and salinity).The finding that river discharge and alongshore wave-driven velocity together explain a large amount of the deviation in HuNoV GII concentrations has practical implications for public health monitoring. Both variables are already measured in near real-time by existing infrastructure (IBWC discharge gauge; CDIP wave buoy at the Imperial Beach Pier) and represented in the regional Pathogen Forecast Model currently under development. The substantial unexplained variance (59.2%) indicates that additional factors are important, including the HuNoV loading rate of the Tijuana River itself, contributions from the SAB plant at Punta Bandera, and the rate of environmental decay of HuNoV GII.We also found a relationship between our HuNoV measurements and county-measured Enterococcus over the same period (Figure ). While this does not imply a mechanistic relationship between the two fecal indicators, this correspondence suggests that both Enterococcus and HuNoV were largely driven by wastewater outflow in the region. It also raises the possibility of estimating extant environmental HuNoV concentrations from more common and cost-effective Enterococcus measurements, although additional data would be required to determine whether this correlation persists over multiyear seasonal cycles and further along the coastline, and previous work has highlighted the disagreement between molecular (e.g., ddPCR) and culture-based quantification of Enterococcus (e.g., with the Enterolert system). A key advantage of using Enterococcus as a proxy for HuNoV is seen in Figure a, where the EPA threshold for HuNoV GII illness probability (assuming mean ingestion) falls well below the median LoB in our study. Larger sample volumes yield lower LoB values; by rearranging eq , we estimate that a 4.1 L sample volume would be required to detect HuNoV GII at a concentration consistent with the EPA threshold (assuming a mean ingestion and not accounting for recovery efficiency).Mean estimates of the probability of swimmer illness, as calculated with a simulation of different doses, infectivity rates, and the average HuNoV concentration, suggest that most locations in the study area would expose swimmers to elevated levels of illness risk (Figure ). Future studies and models that predict swimmer illness risk will also need to evaluate the decay and infectivity properties of HuNoV GII, especially as a function of temperature, salinity, and UV light exposure, which are known to be influential in determining HuNoV persistence in the environment. , If the infectivity of HuNoV GII decreases rapidly due to environmental exposure, the probability of swimmer illness will significantly decrease, especially for the stations farthest from the source. It is important to note that while HuNoV GII is the dominant genogroup in community gastrointestinal illness and in wastewater in North America, HuNoV GI has been more significantly associated with confirmed waterborne outbreaks in published epidemiological analyses, , possibly reflecting its greater stability under environmental conditions encountered in water. The restriction of our monitoring to HuNoV GII, therefore, likely underestimates the total norovirus burden in this environment, and future monitoring campaigns should include HuNoV GI to capture a broader spectrum of waterborne norovirus risks at this site.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHuman noroviruses (“Norwalk viruses”; HuNoV) are the leading cause of gastrointestinal infections worldwide, including millions of cases per year in the United States alone. , HuNoV is considered a public health concern because of its broad range of potential hosts. High rates of mutation − and a low infectious dose contribute to this burden. , Among the strains that infect humans, GII is the most prevalent, followed by GI and GIV. HuNoV infection presents with many symptomsprimarily diarrhea and vomiting , and while most cases resolve without medical intervention, severe outcomes including dehydration, hospitalization, and death can occur, particularly in children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. , The primary mode of HuNoV transmission is the fecal-oral route. Once infected, humans produce and release the virus in their gut, where it is readily excreted. Given this relationship between HuNoV and human waste, environmental contamination by sewage can be a significant mode of transmission. Despite the global health burden of HuNoV and the widespread use of coastal areas for recreation, quantitative monitoring of HuNoV GII in marine coastal environments is exceptionally rare. Most environmental HuNoV studies have focused on freshwater, groundwater, or wastewater treatment plants, with only a handful of studies characterizing concentrations in coastal marine waters. − Early work at Southern California recreational beaches detected HuNoV in 22% of samples at Doheny Beach in Orange County, highlighting the strong spatial heterogeneity driven by proximity to wastewater sources. A separate study consistently detected HuNoV at the mouth of the San Diego River and Tourmaline Creek following storm events. More recent work in Asia has demonstrated that seasonal patterns in enteric virus occurrence in recreational marine waters are driven by a combination of wastewater source shifts and environmental decay. None of these studies have reported sustained weekly monitoring across multiple spatial scales in a persistently wastewater-impacted coastal environment. This is of particular concern in regions with high levels of wastewater pollution, such as the San Diego–Tijuana border region between the US and Mexico. − Broken or overcapacity wastewater infrastructure in this region has been linked to a range of elevated pollutants or their indicators, including fluorescent organic matter, microbial pathogens, organic pollutants, and chemical contaminants found in both water and aerosols. , Despite the chronic pollution, we are not aware of any HuNoV measurements in the Tijuana River and adjacent coastal waters.For the San Diego–Tijuana border region, there is a critical need to quantify how much HuNoV GII is delivered to local beaches, how far it can be transported by coastal hydrodynamics, and whether its concentration varies over seasonal and interannual time scales. Three important public health objectives cannot be met without such quantitative data: (1) the benefit of infrastructure improvements to the Tijuana wastewater system cannot be quantitatively evaluated; (2) routine fecal indicator monitoring (Enterococcus) cannot be rigorously validated as a HuNoV GII (and other enteric pathogen) proxy at this site; and (3) physics-based pathogen forecast models for this region cannot utilize realistic HuNoV GII concentrations as boundary conditions.In this study, we conducted weekly sampling from June to December 2024 across a range of locations near the San Diego–Tijuana border region to quantify environmental reverse transcription digital droplet polymerase chain reaction (RT-ddPCR) counts of HuNoV GII. Using these measurements, we address how environmental HuNoV GII concentrations varied across space and time during our study in this region. We compared our HuNoV GII measurements to concurrent concentrations of Enterococcus, the primary regulatory fecal indicator used to trigger beach closures in the United States. If Enterococcus covaries with HuNoV GII, it may serve as a cost-effective proxy for viral pathogen risk within the existing monitoring infrastructure. Next, we explore variations in HuNoV GII as a function of Tijuana River discharge and the wave-driven, depth-averaged current flowing parallel to the shoreline within the surfzone (hereinafter “alongshore wave-driven velocity”), two factors known to modulate the alongshore transport and dilution of pollutants from sewage sources in this region. − Last, we undertake a risk assessment based on observed HuNoV concentrations and place these observations in the context of the EPA safe swimming guideline of 32 illnesses per 1000 swimmers. Together, these analyses provide the first quantitative, empirically grounded picture of the HuNoV landscape along this stretch of the US–Mexico coast, with direct implications for public health monitoring, infrastructure evaluation, and predictive modeling of pathogen fate and transport. Site DescriptionThe San Diego–Tijuana border region is located along the west coast of North America at the US–Mexico border. This area spans highly populated cities, the Tijuana River system, and an estuary that connects to the Pacific Ocean just north of the US–Mexico border. This study focuses on sampling conducted along a ∼12 km stretch of the US side of the coastal ocean border region from 19 June 2024 through 30 December 2024.Wastewater from Tijuana is collected by the South Bay International Wastewater Treatment Plant (SBIWTP), operated by the International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC) at the US–Mexico border. If the infrastructure is functional and the flow rate is lower than the treatment plant’s capacity, the water is treated and sent offshore in a pipe to be discharged at the 30 m isobath. However, if there is an infrastructure failure or if flow rates exceed the treatment plant’s capacityfor example, during periods of high rainfall and runoffthe wastewater is released directly into the Tijuana River. It is then carried downstream across the border, into the Tijuana Estuary, and eventually makes its way to the coastal ocean. The IBWC flow gauge directly measures the amount of water that is not being treated and is being discharged into the river; we report this as the river discharge variable in this study. This water is a mixture of raw wastewater and runoff. Thus, the concentration of wastewater can vary with the total discharged amount.Intermittent sources of wastewater enter the lower reaches of the Tijuana River through canyons and collectors, principally Goat Canyon and Smuggler’s Gulch. These channels are not continuously gauged, and the discharges are event-driven (often following rainfall or following infrastructure failures). These sources are considered to be a minor component of the Tijuana River discharge, though they can carry a high concentration of untreated sewage.The San Antonio de Los Buenos (SAB) treatment plant, located ∼10 km south of the US–Mexico border near Punta Bandera, represents another major discharge site. At this location, partially or inadequately treated wastewater is discharged directly onto the beach due to the outfall from SAB. Wastewater from Punta Bandera frequently impacts the study region and represents a significant secondary source of contamination. While there have been some improvements to this treatment facility since our study concluded, the SAB plant is distinct from the SBIWTP at the border and represents an independent wastewater loading pathway to the study area.Site names in this study follow San Diego County monitoring conventions. The prefix “PP” denotes the Playa Punta/Border Fence area adjacent to the river mouth; “IB” denotes Imperial Beach; and “EH” denotes Enhanced Hazard stations maintained by San Diego County. Numeric suffixes indicate cross-shore position: no suffix indicates a shoreline or beach sample, “_1′′ indicates a nearshore station, and “_2′′ indicates an offshore station. Thes…

title_original: Human Norovirus GII is Widespread in the Coastal Marine Waters of the San Diego–Tijuana (US–Mexico) Border Region

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the presence and distribution of human norovirus GII in coastal marine waters of the San Diego–Tijuana border region, addressing the need to understand its environmental persistence and potential for transmission in this area.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A six-month ddPCR-based monitoring campaign was conducted in the Tijuana River Estuary and adjacent coastal ocean, focusing on sampling along a ∼12 km stretch of the US side of the coastal ocean border region from 19 June 2024 through 30 December 2024. Wastewater from Tijuana is collected by the South Bay International Wastewater Treatment Plant (SBIWTP), operated by the International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC), and carried downstream into the Tijuana Estuary and eventually to the coastal ocean.
analysis.methods: HuNoV GII concentrations were quantified using digital droplet PCR (ddPCR), with statistical analysis of spatial trends requiring per-sample analysis of the limit of blank (LoB). The study also evaluated sample recovery using a MuNoV spike and compared counts from GMM-based procedures with Bio-Rad QuantaSoft software.
analysis.main_results: From June to December 2024, average HuNoV concentrations varied across several orders of magnitude between sampling locations. The greatest average concentrations exceeded 105 copies L–1 at the shoreline location closest to the river mouth (PP-010), while other shoreline locations had mean values of approximately 104 copies L–1. Offshore locations had average values ranging from 102–103 copies L–1. The mean sample recovery from the MuNoV spike was 23.8 ± 5.3%, with no significant difference between samples collected at the river mouth and Silver Strand State Park Campground. Inhibition of RT-ddPCR was generally low, with only beach samples significantly different from the nuclease-free water control in the eluent fraction.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that HuNoV concentrations were highest at the river source and shoreline, decreasing with both cross-shore and along-shore distance. These spatial gradients align with expectations and previous physical models predicting wastewater discharge patterns in the region.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the environmental persistence of HuNoV GII in coastal waters and its potential for transmission in polluted areas, informing public health strategies for monitoring and mitigating viral spread in the San Diego–Tijuana border region.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on wastewater discharge data and the lack of continuous monitoring of the intermittent sources. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on a six-month monitoring campaign with spatial and temporal sampling, but the results are supported by statistical analysis and comparison with previous studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the spatial and temporal distribution of human norovirus GII (HuNoV GII) in the coastal marine waters of the San Diego–Tijuana border region. The research aimed to address the need for understanding HuNoV GII's environmental persistence and transmission risks in this area. A six-month ddPCR-based monitoring campaign was conducted in the Tijuana River Estuary and adjacent coastal ocean, focusing on a ∼12 km stretch of the US side. HuNoV GII concentrations were quantified using digital droplet PCR, with sample recovery evaluated using a MuNoV spike. Results showed that concentrations were highest at the river source and shoreline, decreasing with both cross-shore and along-shore distance. The study found that the mean sample recovery was 23.8 ± 5.3%, with no significant difference between river mouth and Silver Strand State Park samples. Inhibition of RT-ddPCR was generally low, with only beach samples significantly different from the nuclease-free water control. These findings align with physical models predicting wastewater discharge patterns in the region, highlighting the environmental persistence of HuNoV GII and its potential for transmission in coastal waters. The evidence is moderate, based on a six-month monitoring campaign with spatial and temporal sampling, but the results are supported by statistical analysis and comparison with previous studies.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们在蒂华纳河河口及相邻的沿海海洋区域开展了一项为期六个月的基于数字微滴PCR(ddPCR)的监测活动,重点关注2024年6月19日至12月30日期间在美国一侧沿海海洋边境地区的约12公里范围内的采样。蒂华纳的污水由南湾国际污水处理 治疗 植物(SBIWTP)收集,该植物由国际边界水委员会(IBWC)运营,并将污水输送到蒂华纳河口,最终流入沿海海洋。
elements_zh.methods: 使用数字微滴PCR(ddPCR)对HuNoV GII的浓度进行量化,并通过分析每个样本的空白限值(LoB)来统计分析空间趋势。本研究还评估了样本回收率,通过添加MuNoV作为标准品,并将基于GMM的方法计数与Bio-Rad QuantaSoft软件的计数进行比较。
elements_zh.main_results: 从 2024 年 6 月到 12 月,采样地点之间的 HuNoV 平均浓度存在几个数量级的差异。在最靠近河口的海岸线位置(PP-010),最大平均浓度超过 105 拷贝 L-1,而其他海岸线位置的平均值约为 104 拷贝 L-1。近海地点的平均值为 102-103 份 L-1。MuNoV 峰值的平均样本回收率为 23.8 ± 5.3%,在河口和银线州立公园露营地收集的样本之间没有显着差异。RT-ddPCR 的抑制通常较低,只有海滩样品的洗脱液部分与无核酸酶水对照存在显着差异。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究发现,HuNoV GII的浓度在河源和岸边最高,随着离岸距离和沿岸距离的增加而降低。这些空间梯度符合预期,并与之前预测该地区污水排放模式的物理模型一致。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现突显了HuNoV GII在沿海水域中的环境持久性及其在污染区域中潜在的传播,为圣地亚哥-蒂华纳边境地区的公共卫生策略提供了监测和减少病毒传播的依据。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于依赖污水排放数据,并且缺乏对间歇性污染源的持续监测。证据强度中等,因为它是基于为期六个月的监测活动,包括空间和时间采样,但研究结果得到了统计分析和与以往研究的比较的支持。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the presence and distribution of human norovirus GII in coastal marine waters of the San Diego–Tijuana border region, addressing the need to understand its environmental persistence and potential for transmission in this area.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A six-month ddPCR-based monitoring campaign was conducted in the Tijuana River Estuary and adjacent coastal ocean, focusing on sampling along a ∼12 km stretch of the US side of the coastal ocean border region from 19 June 2024 through 30 December 2024. Wastewater from Tijuana is collected by the South Bay International Wastewater Treatment Plant (SBIWTP), operated by the International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC), and carried downstream into the Tijuana Estuary and eventually to the coastal ocean.
analysis_en.methods: HuNoV GII concentrations were quantified using digital droplet PCR (ddPCR), with statistical analysis of spatial trends requiring per-sample analysis of the limit of blank (LoB). The study also evaluated sample recovery using a MuNoV spike and compared counts from GMM-based procedures with Bio-Rad QuantaSoft software.
analysis_en.main_results: From June to December 2024, average HuNoV concentrations varied across several orders of magnitude between sampling locations. The greatest average concentrations exceeded 105 copies L–1 at the shoreline location closest to the river mouth (PP-010), while other shoreline locations had mean values of approximately 104 copies L–1. Offshore locations had average values ranging from 102–103 copies L–1. The mean sample recovery from the MuNoV spike was 23.8 ± 5.3%, with no significant difference between samples collected at the river mouth and Silver Strand State Park Campground. Inhibition of RT-ddPCR was generally low, with only beach samples significantly different from the nuclease-free water control in the eluent fraction.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that HuNoV concentrations were highest at the river source and shoreline, decreasing with both cross-shore and along-shore distance. These spatial gradients align with expectations and previous physical models predicting wastewater discharge patterns in the region.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the environmental persistence of HuNoV GII in coastal waters and its potential for transmission in polluted areas, informing public health strategies for monitoring and mitigating viral spread in the San Diego–Tijuana border region.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on wastewater discharge data and the lack of continuous monitoring of the intermittent sources. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on a six-month monitoring campaign with spatial and temporal sampling, but the results are supported by statistical analysis and comparison with previous studies.

title_zh: 人类 诺如病毒 GII 在圣地亚哥-蒂华纳(美墨边境)沿海海域广泛分布
source_body_en: We conducted a six-month ddPCR-based monitoring campaign in the Tijuana River Estuary and adjacent coastal ocean to quantify HuNoV GII’s spatial and temporal distribution. These findings establish HuNoV GII as a persistent, spatially structured contaminant in this transboundary system and provide a baseline for tracking wastewater infrastructure improvements and informing pathogen risk forecasting models under development.Keywords: environmental pathogens, sewage contamination, gastrointestinal illness, human norovirus, public health Materials and MethodsSite DescriptionThe San Diego–Tijuana border region is located along the west coast of North America at the US–Mexico border. This study focuses on sampling conducted along a ∼12 km stretch of the US side of the coastal ocean border region from 19 June 2024 through 30 December 2024.Wastewater from Tijuana is collected by the South Bay International Wastewater Treatment Plant (SBIWTP), operated by the International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC) at the US–Mexico border. The IBWC flow gauge directly measures the amount of water that is not being treated and is being discharged into the river; we report this as the river discharge variable in this study. AbstractHuman norovirus GII (HuNoV GII) causes millions of gastrointestinal infections annually and persists for days to weeks in marine waters after wastewater discharge, raising transmission concerns in polluted coastal regions such as the San Diego–Tijuana border between the US and Mexico. This is one of the first such spatially and temporally resolved studies in a coastal marine environment. Mean concentrations were ∼102 copies L–1, reaching > 105 copies L–1 near the mouth of the Tijuana River. HuNoV GII declined with increasing distance from shore and the pollution...

title: Systematic functional, genomic, and safety evaluation of food-derived anti-human norovirus candidate Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus YQ001
abstract: Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus YQ001 is a yogurt-derived strain previously reported to bind GII.4 human norovirus (HuNoV) and inhibit viral replication in zebrafish larvae. Here, its in vitro probiotic properties and preliminary safety were evaluated together with whole-genome analysis. The 2.87-Mb genome (46.67% GC; 2757 coding sequences) shared 97.66% average nucleotide identity with L. rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103. L. rhamnosus YQ001 showed acid and bile tolerance, retaining approximately 30% survival after 3 h at pH 2.0 and over 40% after 4 h in 0.2% bile salts. During sequential simulated gastrointestinal digestion, L. rhamnosus YQ001 retained 35.98% survival after the gastric phase and 45.06% after the intestinal phase. L. rhamnosus YQ001 showed over 90% auto-aggregation at 24 h, while its cell-free supernatant exhibited DPPH and ABTS radical-scavenging activities of 85.17% and 76.35%, respectively. Antibacterial activity detected by agar diffusion was abolished after pH neutralization, indicating that the observed inhibition was largely pH-dependent under the tested conditions. L. rhamnosus YQ001 was non-hemolytic and negative for gelatinase and nitroreductase activities. Overall, the phenotypic and genomic findings support the probiotic potential of L. rhamnosus YQ001, while further strain-specific functional and safety evaluation is warranted.

Whole-genome analysis revealed its genetic similarity to other Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus strains. The findings suggest potential probiotic use for norovirus infection, though further strain-specific functional and safety evaluation is required. The study's limitations include reliance on in vitro data and lack of clinical testing, which may affect the generalizability of the results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估一种从酸奶中分离的乳酸乳球菌YZQ001的益生菌特性和安全性,该菌株此前报道可结合GII.4人类诺如病毒(HuNoV)并在斑马鱼幼鱼中抑制病毒复制。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究评估了乳酸乳球菌YZQ001的体外益生菌特性和初步安全性,以及其全基因组分析,未指定特定的研究设计或人群。
elements_zh.methods: 通过体外试验评估了乳酸乳球菌YZQ001的益生菌特性,包括酸和胆盐耐受性、自聚集能力和自由基清除能力。进行了全基因组分析以比较其与其他菌株的遗传特征。
elements_zh.main_results: 乳酸乳球菌YZQ001表现出酸和胆盐耐受性,在pH 2.0条件下3小时后存活率约为30%,在0.2%胆盐中4小时后存活率超过40%。在连续模拟胃肠消化过程中,其在胃部消化阶段后存活率为35.98%,在肠道消化阶段后存活率为45.06%。该菌株在24小时后表现出超过90%的自聚集能力,并分别表现出85.17%和76.35%的DPPH和ABTS自由基清除能力。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 表型和基因组研究结果表明,乳酸乳球菌YZQ001具有作为益生菌的潜力,尽管需要进一步进行菌株特异性功能和安全性评估。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为乳酸乳球菌YZQ001作为诺如病毒感染的益生菌候选菌株的使用提供了初步支持,可能对未来该领域的研究和开发提供参考。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于体外评估,未包括临床或体内测试,这可能影响研究结果的普遍适用性。由于缺乏全面的安全性和有效性数据,证据强度中等。

abstract_zh: 乳酸乳球菌YZQ001是一种从酸奶中分离的菌株,此前报道可结合GII.4人类诺如病毒(HuNoV)并在斑马鱼幼鱼中抑制病毒复制。本研究对其体外益生菌特性及初步安全性进行了评估,并进行了全基因组分析。该菌株的全基因组为2.87 Mb(GC含量46.67%;包含2757个编码序列),与乳酸乳球菌GG ATCC 53103的平均核苷酸同源性为97.66%。乳酸乳球菌YZQ001表现出酸和胆盐耐受性,在pH 2.0条件下3小时后存活率约为30%,在0.2%胆盐中4小时后存活率超过40%。在连续模拟胃肠消化过程中,乳酸乳球菌YZQ001在胃部消化阶段后存活率为35.98%,在肠道消化阶段后存活率为45.06%。该菌株在24小时后表现出超过90%的自聚集能力,其无细胞培养上清液表现出85.17%的DPPH自由基清除能力和76.35%的ABTS自由基清除能力。通过琼脂扩散法检测到的抗菌活性在pH中和后被消除,表明在测试条件下观察到的抑制作用主要依赖于pH值。乳酸乳球菌YZQ001不溶血,且不表现出明胶酶和硝基还原酶活性。总体而言,表型和基因组研究结果支持乳酸乳球菌YZQ001作为益生菌的潜力,但需要进一步进行菌株特异性功能和安全性评估。

full_text: AbstractFecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an effective therapy for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI) and is increasingly explored for other dysbiosis-related disorders. However, its implementation as a regulated therapeutic strategy requires robust donor screening, biosafety frameworks, and standardized processing workflows. Here, we describe the establishment of the first fecal microbiota biobank in southern Brazil and evaluate the incorporation of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary layer of donor characterization and safety assessment. A structured donor selection pipeline based on international guidelines was implemented, integrating clinical screening, biochemical and serological testing, and microbiological analyses. Of 100 screened candidates, only four donors met all eligibility criteria and were included in the biobank, highlighting the stringency of the selection process. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed a diverse resistome across all donors, including a shared core set of resistance genes alongside marked interindividual variability. Dominant resistance determinants included tetracycline-associated genes, ermF, CfxA-type β-lactamases, and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, which were associated with specific gut taxa. Genomic context analysis further identified four ARG-containing contigs with features compatible with potential mobility, although active horizontal gene transfer was beyond the scope of this study. Notably, tet(Q) and ermF were predominantly associated with Bacteroides fragilis, supporting its role as a reservoir of resistance determinants in the gut microbiota. These findings support the use of metagenomic profiling as a complementary approach to donor characterization and risk assessment rather than as a standalone criterion for donor exclusion. Overall, this study provides a framework for microbiota biobank implementation and highlights the potential of metagenomic analysis to complement conventional biosafety screening in FMT.Keywords: antimicrobial resistance, biosafety, fecal microbiota transplantation, metagenomics, microbiota-based therapies, resistome 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study designThis study was designed as a descriptive and methodological investigation aimed at establishing the first fecal microbiota biobank in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, intended to support the future clinical use of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in selected diseases. The study was structured in three main sequential phases: (i) development of donor screening tools based on international guidelines; (ii) implementation of a clinical and laboratory-based donor selection pipeline; and (iii) exploratory incorporation of metagenomic analysis of donor’s fecal microbiota.2.2.Development of donor screening questionnaire and testing pipelineInitially, a comprehensive literature review was performed to identify and compare current recommendations for FMT donor selection and biosafety. This review focused on three core components: clinical exclusion criteria, blood and serological testing, and microbiological screening of fecal samples. The screening tests developed by major national and international working groups were analyzed and compared, including those from the IAG HC-UFMG (Terra et al., 2020), the Netherlands Working Group (Terveer et al., 2020), the International Consensus Conference on FMT (Cammarota et al., 2019), the European FMT Working Group (Cammarota et al., 2017), and the Australian Consensus (Haifer et al., 2020). Based on this comparative analysis and additional literature, a customized screening questionnaire and testing pipeline were developed and implemented in the present work (Supplementary Tables 1, 2).2.3.Donor recruitment and clinical screeningDonor recruitment was conducted between July and September 2023 through public calls and institutional communication channels. Eligible volunteers were invited to complete a structured clinical screening questionnaire based on international FMT guidelines. Eligible donors were required to be between 18 and 50 years of age. Candidates presenting one or more exclusion criteria were not allowed to proceed to subsequent screening steps. Exclusion criteria included, but were not limited to, recent antibiotic use, chronic gastrointestinal diseases, metabolic or autoimmune disorders, recent infectious diseases, high-risk behaviors, and abnormal bowel habits. In addition, the clinical screening questionnaire included questions regarding illicit drug use, chronic medication use, occupational exposure to hazardous substances, and other potential risk factors associated with biological, toxicological or chemical exposure.2.4.Laboratory testsCandidates who met the clinical eligibility criteria were submitted to a comprehensive laboratory screening protocol, designed to assess general health status and exclude infectious agents potentially transmissible through fecal microbiota transplantation. Blood-based analyses included a complete blood count, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), renal and hepatic function markers (urea, creatinine, AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin), metabolic and nutritional parameters (glucose, vitamin B12, folic acid, vitamin D), and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein). Serological screening comprised tests for HIV types I and II, hepatitis A (IgM/IgG), hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG/IgM), hepatitis C (anti-HCV), human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV I/II), cytomegalovirus (IgG/IgM), and Epstein–Barr virus (IgG/IgM).Fecal samples were analyzed for enteric pathogens using conventional microbiological methods and molecular assays. These included coproculture and PCR-based detection of Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin A/B, rotavirus, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, herpes simplex virus I and II (IgG and IgM), and a multiplex PCR panel (FilmArray®) targeting bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens, such as Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., Shigella/EIEC, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, C. difficile, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, norovirus GI/GII, astrovirus, sapovirus, and adenovirus F40/41. Only candidates presenting normal results across all clinical, serological, biochemical, and microbiological tests were considered eligible donors for inclusion in the biobank.2.5.Processing and storage of fecal materialFecal material from eligible donors was processed under controlled laboratory conditions following standardized operating procedures. Prior to collection, eligible donors received a standardized collection kit containing sterile collection containers, disposable gloves, identification labels, and detailed written instructions describing the collection procedure and emphasizing aseptic handling practices. Donors were instructed to avoid contact between fecal material and external surfaces by using a single-use stool collection device (ColOff®) and to maintain samples refrigerated until transport to the laboratory. Samples were collected from donors’ homes shortly after evacuation and transported to the laboratory in insulated coolers containing ice packs. The total time elapsed between stool passage and laboratory processing did not exceed 6 hours. Upon arrival, samples were processed under atmospheric conditions in a laminar flow cabinet. Fecal material was homogenized in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), filtered through a sterile sieve to remove particulate debris, aliquoted into 10 mL fractions, and stored at −80 °C until use. All samples were labeled and documented to ensure traceability, and storage conditions were continuously monitored.2.6.Shotgun metagenomics sequencingTotal genomic DNA from fecal samples obtained from eligible donors was extracted using the Quick-DNATM HMW MagBead Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), while DNA purity was assessed by NanoVue spectrophotometry (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) based on the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios. DNA integrity was evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis prior to library preparation.Metagenomic sequencing libraries were prepared using the Rapid Barcoding Kit 24 v14 (SQK-RBK114.24; Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK), pooled, and sequenced for 48 h on a MinION device using an R10.4.1 flow cell. Raw reads were basecalled and demultiplexed using Guppy v4.3.0 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). No extraction blank or negative sequencing control was included in the sequencing workflow.2.7.Identification of antimicrobial resistance genesAntimicrobial resistance determinants were identified directly from sequencing reads using the command-line version of the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI, v6.0.3) against the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD). Read quality was evaluated using NanoPlot v1.40.0, followed by quality filtering using NanoFilt v2.8.0, retaining reads with a minimum mean quality score of Q10 and a minimum length of 500 bp. Only Perfect and Strict hits were retained for downstream analyses, whereas Loose hits were excluded to reduce the likelihood of false-positive assignments. Gene presence/absence, relative abundance, and cumulative abundance profiles were generated for descriptive comparisons across samples using R v4.3.2. Due to the exploratory nature of the study and the limited number of samples, no inferential statistical analyses were performed.2.8.Genomic context and potential mobility of resistance determinantsTo characterize the genomic context of ARGs and assess their potential mobility, sequencing reads were filtered at minimum mean quality score of Q8 and a minimum length of 1000 bp and were assembled using Flye v2.9.6. The resulting contigs were screened for ARGs using ABRicate v1.4.0 against the CARD database (≥90% identity and ≥80% coverage), and ARG-containing contigs were further characterized for plasmid association and mobility-related features using geNomad v1.12.0, MOB-suite v3.1.9, Bakta v1.9.4, and ISEScan v1.7.3. To assess sequence support for candidate contigs and ARGs, the reads were mapped to the corresponding Flye assemblies using Minimap2 v2.31, and read depth was calculated with SAMtools v1.23.1.2.9.Data availabilityThe raw sequencing data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1499213.2.10.Ethical considerationsThe study was approved by the institutional review board under process number CAAE: 42603020.0.0000.0121. All participants provided written informed consent prior to sample collection and laboratory analyses. 2.1.Study designThis study was designed as a descriptive and methodological investigation aimed at establishing the first fecal microbiota biobank in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, intended to support the future clinical use of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in selected diseases. The study was structured in three main sequential phases: (i) development of donor screening tools based on international guidelines; (ii) implementation of a clinical and laboratory-based donor selection pipeline; and (iii) exploratory incorporation of metagenomic analysis of donor’s fecal microbiota. 2.5.Processing and storage of fecal materialFecal material from eligible donors was processed under controlled laboratory conditions following standardized operating procedures. Prior to collection, eligible donors received a standardized collection kit containing sterile collection containers, disposable gloves, identification labels, and detailed written instructions describing the collection procedure and emphasizing aseptic handling practices. Donors were instructed to avoid contact between fecal material and external surfaces by using a single-use stool collection device (ColOff®) and to maintain samples refrigerated until transport to the laboratory. Samples were collected from donors’ homes shortly after evacuation and transported to the laboratory in insulated coolers containing ice packs. The total time elapsed between stool passage and laboratory processing did not exceed 6 hours. Upon arrival, samples were processed under atmospheric conditions in a laminar flow cabinet. Fecal material was homogenized in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), filtered through a sterile sieve to remove particulate debris, aliquoted into 10 mL fractions, and stored at −80 °C until use. All samples were labeled and documented to ensure traceability, and storage conditions were continuously monitored. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frabi.2026.1905540/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 3.Results3.1.Donor recruitment and clinical eligibilityA total of 100 candidates were included in the clinical screening questionnaire during the recruitment period. Of these, 6 candidates met the clinical eligibility criteria and were referred to laboratory screening. Following biochemical, serological, and microbiological screening, two additional candidates were excluded, one due to the detection of toxigenic C. difficile by multiplex PCR (FilmArray®), while another candidate did not complete the laboratory screening process. Therefore, four participants were ultimately considered eligible for fecal microbiota donation and inclusion in the biobank. The donor selection workflow and the main exclusion criteria identified are illustrated in Figure 1. The demographic characteristics of the eligible donors are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.Figure 1Flowchart illustrating the multistep donor selection process.Flowchart detailing donor screening for a biobank. From one hundred questionnaires, six proceed to clinical evaluation and laboratory testing. Two are excluded due to C. difficile detection and incomplete screening, leading to four eligible donors. Main exclusion criteria are also listed.3.2.Resistome profile characterizationSequencing generated 7.09 Gb of data across all samples (5.44 million reads; N50 = 2.55 kb), with read accuracy ranging from 79.6% to 84.7%, indicating overall good sequencing performance. Shotgun metagenomic analysis of fecal samples from eligible donors identified 180 different resistance-related gene entries in CARD dataset. Detection frequency varied between samples, with 137 genes identified in Sample 1, 87 in Sample 2, 103 in Sample 3, and 134 in Sample 4. Of these, only 58 were consistently detected in all samples, whereas 122 showed partial occurrence in different samples (Figure 2A). To improve biological interpretability, detected entries were grouped into two major categories: ARGs, comprising canonical resistance genes whose presence is directly associated with antimicrobial resistance phenotypes (n= 100), and variant-dependent loci, corresponding to conserved chromosomal targets in which resistance is typically mediated by specific sequence variants rather than gene presence alone (e.g., rRNA genes, gyrA/parC/parE, and rpoB-associated loci) (n=80). Among consensus genes, only eleven were classified as canonical ARGs (Core resistome), including APH(3’)-IIIa, CfxA2, CfxA3, ErmF, mefA, AlaS and five tetracycline resistance determinants (tet (32), tet (40), tet(O), tet(Q), and tet(W)).Figure 2UpSet plot showing the intersection (number) of resistance-related genes detected across the four samples. The bar plot (top) indicates the number of genes shared among specific combinations of samples, while the dot matrix (bottom) represents the corresponding sample intersections. A total of 58 genes were detected in all four samples, while additional genes were shared among subsets of samples or were sample-specific (A). Horizontal bars (left) indicate the total number of genes detected in each individual sample. Classification of resistance-related entries according to functional category (B).Panel A shows an intersection bar chart and matrix illustrating shared gene counts among four samples, with the highest intersection grouping sharing fifty-eight genes. Horizontal bars display the number of genes detected per sample. Panel B is a horizontal bar chart comparing counts of ARG with one hundred entries and variant-dependent loci with eighty entries.3.3.Taxonomic distribution and abundance of dominant antibiotic resistance genesThe taxonomic distribution of the most abundant ARGs across samples is shown in Figure 3A. A consistent set of dominant resistance genes was observed across all samples, with tet(Q), tet(W), tet(O), ErmF, and CfxA2 representing the most prominent determinants. These genes were strongly associated with specific bacterial taxa, indicating clear links between resistome composition and microbiota structure. In particular, tet(Q) was predominantly associated with Bacteroides fragilis, while tet(W) was mainly linked to Bifidobacterium longum. The gene tet(O) was primarily associated with Campylobacter jejuni, whereas ErmF was also largely attributed to Bacteroides fragilis. In contrast, CfxA2 was associated with Prevotella intermedia, highlighting additional taxonomic contributors to β-lactam resistance.Figure 3(A) Individual bar plots for each sample showing the distribution (%) of the 12 most abundant resistance genes, categorized by their associated bacterial taxa.
