full_text_sections.methods: 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study designThis study was designed as a descriptive and methodological investigation aimed at establishing the first fecal microbiota biobank in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, intended to support the future clinical use of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in selected diseases. The study was structured in three main sequential phases: (i) development of donor screening tools based on international guidelines; (ii) implementation of a clinical and laboratory-based donor selection pipeline; and (iii) exploratory incorporation of metagenomic analysis of donor’s fecal microbiota.2.2.Development of donor screening questionnaire and testing pipelineInitially, a comprehensive literature review was performed to identify and compare current recommendations for FMT donor selection and biosafety. This review focused on three core components: clinical exclusion criteria, blood and serological testing, and microbiological screening of fecal samples. The screening tests developed by major national and international working groups were analyzed and compared, including those from the IAG HC-UFMG (Terra et al., 2020), the Netherlands Working Group (Terveer et al., 2020), the International Consensus Conference on FMT (Cammarota et al., 2019), the European FMT Working Group (Cammarota et al., 2017), and the Australian Consensus (Haifer et al., 2020). Based on this comparative analysis and additional literature, a customized screening questionnaire and testing pipeline were developed and implemented in the present work (Supplementary Tables 1, 2).2.3.Donor recruitment and clinical screeningDonor recruitment was conducted between July and September 2023 through public calls and institutional communication channels. Eligible volunteers were invited to complete a structured clinical screening questionnaire based on international FMT guidelines. Eligible donors were required to be between 18 and 50 years of age. Candidates presenting one or more exclusion criteria were not allowed to proceed to subsequent screening steps. Exclusion criteria included, but were not limited to, recent antibiotic use, chronic gastrointestinal diseases, metabolic or autoimmune disorders, recent infectious diseases, high-risk behaviors, and abnormal bowel habits. In addition, the clinical screening questionnaire included questions regarding illicit drug use, chronic medication use, occupational exposure to hazardous substances, and other potential risk factors associated with biological, toxicological or chemical exposure.2.4.Laboratory testsCandidates who met the clinical eligibility criteria were submitted to a comprehensive laboratory screening protocol, designed to assess general health status and exclude infectious agents potentially transmissible through fecal microbiota transplantation. Blood-based analyses included a complete blood count, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), renal and hepatic function markers (urea, creatinine, AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin), metabolic and nutritional parameters (glucose, vitamin B12, folic acid, vitamin D), and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein). Serological screening comprised tests for HIV types I and II, hepatitis A (IgM/IgG), hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG/IgM), hepatitis C (anti-HCV), human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV I/II), cytomegalovirus (IgG/IgM), and Epstein–Barr virus (IgG/IgM).Fecal samples were analyzed for enteric pathogens using conventional microbiological methods and molecular assays. These included coproculture and PCR-based detection of Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin A/B, rotavirus, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, herpes simplex virus I and II (IgG and IgM), and a multiplex PCR panel (FilmArray®) targeting bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens, such as Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., Shigella/EIEC, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, C. difficile, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, norovirus GI/GII, astrovirus, sapovirus, and adenovirus F40/41. Only candidates presenting normal results across all clinical, serological, biochemical, and microbiological tests were considered eligible donors for inclusion in the biobank.2.5.Processing and storage of fecal materialFecal material from eligible donors was processed under controlled laboratory conditions following standardized operating procedures. Prior to collection, eligible donors received a standardized collection kit containing sterile collection containers, disposable gloves, identification labels, and detailed written instructions describing the collection procedure and emphasizing aseptic handling practices. Donors were instructed to avoid contact between fecal material and external surfaces by using a single-use stool collection device (ColOff®) and to maintain samples refrigerated until transport to the laboratory. Samples were collected from donors’ homes shortly after evacuation and transported to the laboratory in insulated coolers containing ice packs. The total time elapsed between stool passage and laboratory processing did not exceed 6 hours. Upon arrival, samples were processed under atmospheric conditions in a laminar flow cabinet. Fecal material was homogenized in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), filtered through a sterile sieve to remove particulate debris, aliquoted into 10 mL fractions, and stored at −80 °C until use. All samples were labeled and documented to ensure traceability, and storage conditions were continuously monitored.2.6.Shotgun metagenomics sequencingTotal genomic DNA from fecal samples obtained from eligible donors was extracted using the Quick-DNATM HMW MagBead Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), while DNA purity was assessed by NanoVue spectrophotometry (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) based on the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios. DNA integrity was evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis prior to library preparation.Metagenomic sequencing libraries were prepared using the Rapid Barcoding Kit 24 v14 (SQK-RBK114.24; Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK), pooled, and sequenced for 48 h on a MinION device using an R10.4.1 flow cell. Raw reads were basecalled and demultiplexed using Guppy v4.3.0 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). No extraction blank or negative sequencing control was included in the sequencing workflow.2.7.Identification of antimicrobial resistance genesAntimicrobial resistance determinants were identified directly from sequencing reads using the command-line version of the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI, v6.0.3) against the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD). Read quality was evaluated using NanoPlot v1.40.0, followed by quality filtering using NanoFilt v2.8.0, retaining reads with a minimum mean quality score of Q10 and a minimum length of 500 bp. Only Perfect and Strict hits were retained for downstream analyses, whereas Loose hits were excluded to reduce the likelihood of false-positive assignments. Gene presence/absence, relative abundance, and cumulative abundance profiles were generated for descriptive comparisons across samples using R v4.3.2. Due to the exploratory nature of the study and the limited number of samples, no inferential statistical analyses were performed.2.8.Genomic context and potential mobility of resistance determinantsTo characterize the genomic context of ARGs and assess their potential mobility, sequencing reads were filtered at minimum mean quality score of Q8 and a minimum length of 1000 bp and were assembled using Flye v2.9.6. The resulting contigs were screened for ARGs using ABRicate v1.4.0 against the CARD database (≥90% identity and ≥80% coverage), and ARG-containing contigs were further characterized for plasmid association and mobility-related features using geNomad v1.12.0, MOB-suite v3.1…
full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Donor recruitment and clinical eligibilityA total of 100 candidates were included in the clinical screening questionnaire during the recruitment period. Of these, 6 candidates met the clinical eligibility criteria and were referred to laboratory screening. Following biochemical, serological, and microbiological screening, two additional candidates were excluded, one due to the detection of toxigenic C. difficile by multiplex PCR (FilmArray®), while another candidate did not complete the laboratory screening process. Therefore, four participants were ultimately considered eligible for fecal microbiota donation and inclusion in the biobank. The donor selection workflow and the main exclusion criteria identified are illustrated in Figure 1. The demographic characteristics of the eligible donors are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.Figure 1Flowchart illustrating the multistep donor selection process.Flowchart detailing donor screening for a biobank. From one hundred questionnaires, six proceed to clinical evaluation and laboratory testing. Two are excluded due to C. difficile detection and incomplete screening, leading to four eligible donors. Main exclusion criteria are also listed.3.2.Resistome profile characterizationSequencing generated 7.09 Gb of data across all samples (5.44 million reads; N50 = 2.55 kb), with read accuracy ranging from 79.6% to 84.7%, indicating overall good sequencing performance. Shotgun metagenomic analysis of fecal samples from eligible donors identified 180 different resistance-related gene entries in CARD dataset. Detection frequency varied between samples, with 137 genes identified in Sample 1, 87 in Sample 2, 103 in Sample 3, and 134 in Sample 4. Of these, only 58 were consistently detected in all samples, whereas 122 showed partial occurrence in different samples (Figure 2A). To improve biological interpretability, detected entries were grouped into two major categories: ARGs, comprising canonical resistance genes whose presence is directly associated with antimicrobial resistance phenotypes (n= 100), and variant-dependent loci, corresponding to conserved chromosomal targets in which resistance is typically mediated by specific sequence variants rather than gene presence alone (e.g., rRNA genes, gyrA/parC/parE, and rpoB-associated loci) (n=80). Among consensus genes, only eleven were classified as canonical ARGs (Core resistome), including APH(3’)-IIIa, CfxA2, CfxA3, ErmF, mefA, AlaS and five tetracycline resistance determinants (tet (32), tet (40), tet(O), tet(Q), and tet(W)).Figure 2UpSet plot showing the intersection (number) of resistance-related genes detected across the four samples. The bar plot (top) indicates the number of genes shared among specific combinations of samples, while the dot matrix (bottom) represents the corresponding sample intersections. A total of 58 genes were detected in all four samples, while additional genes were shared among subsets of samples or were sample-specific (A). Horizontal bars (left) indicate the total number of genes detected in each individual sample. Classification of resistance-related entries according to functional category (B).Panel A shows an intersection bar chart and matrix illustrating shared gene counts among four samples, with the highest intersection grouping sharing fifty-eight genes. Horizontal bars display the number of genes detected per sample. Panel B is a horizontal bar chart comparing counts of ARG with one hundred entries and variant-dependent loci with eighty entries.3.3.Taxonomic distribution and abundance of dominant antibiotic resistance genesThe taxonomic distribution of the most abundant ARGs across samples is shown in Figure 3A. A consistent set of dominant resistance genes was observed across all samples, with tet(Q), tet(W), tet(O), ErmF, and CfxA2 representing the most prominent determinants. These genes were strongly associated with specific bacterial taxa, indicating clear links between resistome composition and microbiota structure. In particular, tet(Q) was predominantly associated with Bacteroides fragilis, while tet(W) was mainly linked to Bifidobacterium longum. The gene tet(O) was primarily associated with Campylobacter jejuni, whereas ErmF was also largely attributed to Bacteroides fragilis. In contrast, CfxA2 was associated with Prevotella intermedia, highlighting additional taxonomic contributors to β-lactam resistance.Figure 3(A) Individual bar plots for each sample showing the distribution (%) of the 12 most abundant resistance genes, categorized by their associated bacterial taxa. The color legend indicates taxonomic group carrying the detected ARGs. (B) Stacked bar plot illustrating the distribution of 12 most abundant ARGs across all samples. Each color represents a specific ARG.Panel A shows four grouped bar charts, one for each sample, displaying relative abundance percentages of taxa co-occurring with different antibiotic resistance genes, color-coded by species. Panel B shows a stacked bar graph comparing the relative abundance percentages of different antibiotic resistance genes across the same four samples, with each gene represented by a distinct color.Although these genes were detected across all samples, their proportional abundance varied markedly (Figure 3B). Sample 1 was strongly dominated by tet(Q), which accounted for 34.3% of ARG abundance, followed by ErmF (4.4%) and APH(3’)-IIIa (1.5%). In Sample 2, a more distributed profile was observed, with tet(Q) (9.1%), tet(O) (2.9%), tet (32) (1.9%), and tet (40) (1.7%) contributing to the resistome, along with macrolide resistance genes such as mel (2.2%). Sample 3 showed a more balanced composition, with tet(Q) (15.2%), ErmF (7.3%), tet(W) (7.0%), and CfxA6 (7.6%) representing major contributors. In Sample 4, the dominance of tet(Q) was reduced (4.6%), with increased contributions from tet(W) (6.1%) and ANT(6)-Ib (2.3%), indicating a shift toward a more heterogeneous resistome structure.3.4.Distribution of resistance classes and mechanismsThe resistome was predominantly composed of genes associated with aminoglycoside resistance (32.9%) and tetracycline resistance (28.9%), which together accounted for more than half of the total ARG abundance. Genes related to multidrug resistance also represented a substantial fraction (19.3%), indicating the presence of broad-spectrum resistance determinants. Other classes were detected at lower frequencies, including cephalosporin (5.1%), peptide (3.4%), and elfamycin (2.3%), while macrolide (1.2%) and streptogramin (1.1%) resistance genes contributed minimally to the overall resistome.The functional mechanisms underlying resistance are summarized in Figure 4B. The resistome was strongly dominated by target alteration mechanisms (58.2%), followed by target protection (26.8%), indicating that resistance in these samples is primarily mediated through modifications of antibiotic targets rather than drug degradation or efflux. Enzymatic inactivation mechanisms accounted for 8.4%, while efflux systems contributed 2.9% of the total ARG abundance. Additional mechanisms, including target replacement (1.2%) and unclassified categories (2.4% unknown; 0.1% other), were detected at low frequencies.Figure 4Distribution of resistance genes according to the class of antibiotics (A). Relative abundance of antimicrobial resistance mechanisms identified across the samples (B).Bar chart A shows antibiotic resistance gene categories with aminoglycoside at 32.9 percent, tetracycline at 28.9 percent, and multidrug at 19.3 percent, followed by other categories with lower percentages. Bar chart B presents mechanisms of resistance, with target alteration at 58.2 percent, target protection at 26.8 percent, and additional mechanisms each below 10 percent.3.5.Genomic context supports potential mobility of ARGsBecause the presence of an ARG alone does not indicate its potential for transmission, we further examined the genomic context of resista…
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionA central challenge in FMT implementation worldwide remains the identification of suitable donors. Our findings confirm that donor selection is a highly restrictive process, with only a minority of screened candidates ultimately qualifying for donation. Similar donor approval rates have been reported in international biobanking initiatives, reflecting the stringency required to minimize transmissible risks (Cammarota et al., 2017; Terra et al., 2020). This reinforces the importance of structured, transparent, and reproducible selection workflows as a foundational element of any FMT program. By integrating clinical questionnaires, biochemical and serological testing, and microbiological screening, our workflow aligns with major international guidelines while being operationally feasible within public and private healthcare infrastructures in Brazil (Cammarota et al., 2019). This aspect is particularly relevant in low- and middle-income countries, where the implementation of microbiota-based therapies often faces infrastructural and regulatory barriers.An important contribution of this study is the incorporation of metagenomic sequencing and ARG profiling as an additional source of information for potential donor–recipient selection and risk assessment. In this work, we identified antimicrobial resistance determinants involving clinically relevant antibiotic classes, such as tetracyclines and aminoglycosides, within major members of the gut microbiota, with some occurring in genomic contexts compatible with potential mobilization, even among donors who had undergone rigorous screening.As expected, tetracycline resistance determinants such as tet(Q) and tet(W) were highly prevalent and primarily associated with Bacteroides fragilis and Bifidobacterium longum, respectively, reinforcing the well-established role of these taxa as major reservoirs of tetracycline resistance in the human gut (Shoemaker et al., 2001; Hu et al., 2013). The relatively high abundance of ermF, a gene associated with cross-resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramin B antibiotics (MLSb phenotype), and linked to Bacteroides fragilis, further highlights the role of this species as a reservoir of resistance determinants (Shoemaker et al., 2001). Notably, tet(Q) and ermF occurred together in a chromosomal context containing an IS30 family transposase in Sample 3, sharing features with resistance architectures described in Bacteroides conjugative transposons, including the CTnDOT family, which carries both determinants and contains regions involved in mobilization and conjugative transfer (Shoemaker et al., 2001; Jeters et al., 2009). Other tet(Q) and ARG containing contigs showed complementary features compatible with potential mobility, including proximity to conjugative transfer machinery and association with circular plasmid contigs containing plasmid replication, recombination, or relaxase features. Together, these findings indicate that some resistance determinants occurred in genomic environments compatible with potential mobilization; however, assessment of active horizontal gene transfer was beyond the scope of this study.Although the mobility and horizontal transfer of ARGs are important concerns, the potential for bacteria carrying ARGs in donor feces to persist, translocate, and cause infection in immunocompromised recipients should not be overlooked. This concern is illustrated by the seminal work of DeFilipp et al., which traced the transmission of an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli from donor material to a recipient who subsequently developed bacteremia and died (DeFilipp et al., 2019). In contrast, Woodworth et al. showed that FMT can also promote sustained decolonization of multidrug-resistant organisms, with replacement of baseline ESBL-producing bacteria by susceptible strains (Woodworth et al., 2023). These contrasting findings suggest that the clinical implications of ARGs in FMT depend on the broader donor–recipient context, including the bacterial host and genomic context, but particularly the recipient’s clinical condition and anticipated antimicrobial exposure.In this context, ARG profiling could be used as a complementary layer of donor–recipient assessment rather than as an exclusion criterion, helping to identify cases that may warrant further investigation through phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing or deeper genomic characterization. For example, when clinically relevant resistance determinants are identified, decision makers could consider further investigation of donor feces based on existing guidance for surveillance of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in health care settings (World Health Organization, 2017) This approach could potentially be extended to ESBL producing organisms until further studies specifically evaluating antimicrobial resistance related risks in FMT become available. Future longitudinal studies integrating donor–recipient metagenomic profiling, strain tracking, and clinical outcomes will be important to determine how donor resistance profiles influence the clinical effects of FMT and to refine this risk assessment approach.Beyond donor screening, alternative FMT formulations may provide complementary strategies to improve biosafety. Sterile fecal filtrates and defined microbial consortia, for example, do not rely on the transfer of viable bacterial communities and may therefore reduce some of the risks associated with the introduction of donor-derived organisms (Ott et al., 2017; Feuerstadt et al., 2022). Early clinical evidence suggests that some of these approaches may retain therapeutic efficacy, although their safety and effectiveness require validation in larger and more diverse clinical settings (Ott et al., 2017; Kao et al., 2025). Together, approaches that combine improved biosafety with greater standardization may facilitate the broader and safer implementation of microbiota-based therapies.

title: Pediatric exogenous lipoid pneumonia caused by paraffin oil aspiration: a case report

source_records.title: Pediatric exogenous lipoid pneumonia caused by paraffin oil aspiration: a case report

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: AbstractObjectiveThis case report describes a rare pediatric case of exogenous lipoid pneumonia caused by repeated paraffin oil aspiration and highlights the importance of detailed exposure history, early recognition, and timely intervention.Case presentationWe report the clinical course, diagnostic assessment, treatment, and follow-up of a 4-month-old former preterm infant admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe pneumonia.ResultsRepeated targeted history-taking revealed multiple oral administrations of liquid paraffin with choking episodes. Chest CT showed bilateral consolidation, ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, a crazy-paving pattern, and a focal area of fat attenuation. BALF cytology showed vacuolated histiocytes, although lipid-specific staining was unavailable. Klebsiella aerogenes was detected by throat-swab and BALF targeted next-generation sequencing and was isolated from sputum culture, supporting concomitant lower respiratory tract infection. Following discontinuation of paraffin exposure and multimodal management, the patient showed clinical and radiological improvement.ConclusionExogenous lipoid pneumonia should be considered in infants with treatment-refractory pneumonia and intralesional fat attenuation on CT. Diagnosis requires integration of exposure history, imaging, BALF findings, microbiological evidence, and clinical course. Because several interventions were administered concurrently and long-term follow-up was incomplete, the efficacy of individual treatments and late pulmonary outcomes could not be determined.Keywords: aspiration, exogenous lipid, lipoid pneumonia, paraffin oil, pediatric 3.DiscussionExogenous lipoid pneumonia is a rare noninfectious inflammatory lung disease caused by aspiration or inhalation of exogenous lipids (3, 4). Its presentation is heterogeneous and often overlaps with infectious pneumonia, with cough, sputum production, fever, tachypnea, and dyspnea as common manifestations (1).The patient's previous prematurity and very young corrected age may have increased the risk of aspiration because of immature swallowing, cough reflexes, and suck-swallow-breathing coordination (5–10). During the previous hospitalization, liquid paraffin was given orally by the caregivers using a spoon while the infant was held upright. Brief choking was not recognized as possible aspiration and was not reported to medical personnel. This case emphasizes that coughing or choking during administration of an oily medication to an infant should prompt immediate discontinuation, assessment of aspiration risk, and notification of medical personnel. Once aspirated, paraffin oil may impair mucociliary clearance and surfactant function and may trigger macrophage-mediated alveolar inflammation and, in persistent cases, fibrosis (11–14).ELP was first suspected on September 30, 2024, after clinical and radiological progression despite initial antimicrobial therapy. Infectious pneumonia was initially favored because of fever, leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, bilateral pulmonary opacities, and positive respiratory microbiological findings. Although the initial CT showed a focal fat-attenuation area, the absence of a reported oily substance exposure history limited its immediate interpretation. Repeated targeted history-taking subsequently identified paraffin administration with choking. CT manifestations of lipoid pneumonia include consolidation, ground-glass opacities, nodules, interlobular septal thickening, crazy paving, and intralesional fat attenuation. Lesions are often bilateral and multifocal, with middle- and lower-lobe and dependent posterior predominance in aspiration-related cases; peripheral sparing is not a typical or specific finding (1, 15, 16). A solitary fat-attenuation focus is supportive but not independently diagnostic and should be interpreted with the exposure history and other findings.Several diagnostic limitations should be acknowledged. Lipid-specific staining of BALF, such as Oil Red O or Sudan III staining, was unavailable because of local laboratory limitations. The BALF specimen had undergone routine cytological processing, during which lipid may be dissolved or extracted, and no unfixed residual specimen was available for retrospective staining. Accordingly, the vacuolated histiocytes were considered supportive rather than confirmatory. Lung biopsy was not performed because of its invasiveness and the patient's young age. The diagnosis was therefore clinical, based on the combined exposure history, CT findings, BALF morphology, and clinical course (1, 17–19).Another important consideration was concomitant bacterial lower respiratory tract infection. K. aerogenes was detected by throat-swab tNGS and BALF tNGS and was isolated from sputum culture. The concordant microbiological findings, together with persistent fever, airway secretions, pulmonary moist rales, respiratory deterioration, and bilateral pulmonary opacities, supported clinically significant infection rather than incidental upper-airway colonization. Although procalcitonin levels remained relatively low at 0.28 and 0.22 ng/mL, these values did not exclude bacterial infection in the presence of consistent microbiological and clinical evidence. Prematurity and aspiration-related epithelial injury may also have impaired local pulmonary defense. Clinical and radiological improvement occurred during susceptibility-concordant antimicrobial therapy; however, the relative contributions of bacterial infection and lipid-induced sterile inflammation could not be fully separated (11, 20).No specific guideline or consensus exists for ELP management, and treatment remains largely empirical (21, 22). The main principles are discontinuation of lipid exposure, respiratory support, airway clearance, and removal of aspirated lipid. Bronchoalveolar lavage may help remove lipid material, lipid-containing macrophages, and inflammatory mediators, whereas whole-lung lavage is technically demanding in infants. Corticosteroids have been used to suppress inflammation, although optimal dose and duration remain uncertain. IVIG is not an established or disease-specific treatment for ELP. In this patient, it was administered empirically at a total dose of 2 g/kg as adjunctive immunomodulatory therapy because of severe progressive inflammatory lung injury, concomitant infection, previous prematurity, and concern regarding relative immune immaturity. Evidence supporting IVIG is limited to observational experience, and its independent contribution cannot be determined because bronchoalveolar lavage, corticosteroids, antimicrobial therapy, respiratory support, postural drainage, and IVIG were administered concurrently (21–23).Available follow-up through day 145 showed progressive radiological improvement. However, standardized pulmonary function testing, exercise-tolerance assessment, and imaging beyond day 145 were unavailable after the family relocated to another province. Therefore, residual interstitial abnormalities, later fibrosis, or impaired pulmonary function cannot be completely excluded. Other limitations include the absence of lipid-specific staining and histopathological confirmation, the coexistence of infection and sterile inflammatory injury, and the inability to attribute recovery to any single intervention.In summary, ELP should be considered in infants with treatment-refractory pneumonia, particularly when CT demonstrates intralesional fat attenuation. Detailed and repeated exposure history-taking is essential. In this case, discontinuation of paraffin exposure and multimodal management were associated with clinical and radiological improvement; however, the efficacy of individual interventions, particularly IVIG, cannot be inferred from a single case, and continued long-term follow-up remains important. 1.IntroductionExogenous lipoid pneumonia (ELP) is a rare pulmonary disorder caused by the inhalation or aspiration of vegetable, animal, or mineral oils, resulting in acute or chronic inflammation of the pulmonary interstitium and parenchyma (1, 2). Its manifestations, including cough, tachypnea, fever, and dyspnea, are nonspecific. CT findings such as consolidation, ground-glass opacities, nodules, and a crazy-paving pattern may overlap with infectious pneumonia and other diffuse lung diseases, making delayed diagnosis common (1). Here, we report a former preterm infant with ELP caused by repeated paraffin oil aspiration and complicated by concomitant Klebsiella aerogenes lower respiratory tract infection. This case highlights the importance of repeated targeted history-taking, integrated diagnostic reasoning, and cautious interpretation of treatment response.Table 1Timeline of the clinical course.DateKey clinical findingsAssessment and managementSep 20–24, 2024Hospitalized for adhesive intestinal obstruction. Repeated oral liquid paraffin administration with choking was disclosed later.Conservative management of intestinal obstruction.Sep 24, 2024Admitted with cough, fever, and diarrhea; WBC 18.11 × 109/L, CRP 65.54 mg/L, PCT 0.28 ng/mL; bilateral pulmonary opacities; throat-swab tNGS detected K. aerogenes.Bronchopneumonia and norovirus enteritis initially considered; oxygen, empirical antimicrobials, nebulization, and supportive care.Sep 28, 2024Respiratory deterioration with tachypnea and retractions; PCT 0.22 ng/mL; CT showed bilateral consolidation, ground-glass opacities, septal thickening, crazy paving, and focal fat attenuation.Transferred to PICU; NCPAP, linezolid, meropenem, bronchoscopy, and BAL.Sep 30, 2024Persistent fever, cough, tachypnea, and radiological progression. Repeated history-taking revealed multiple paraffin administrations with choking. BALF showed vacuolated histiocytes.ELP first suspected and clinically diagnosed; paraffin exposure discontinued; corticosteroids, postural drainage, respiratory support, targeted antimicrobials, and empirical adjunctive IVIG continued.Oct 4–20, 2024Respiratory status stabilized; no cough or tachypnea at discharge.Respiratory support downgraded; discharged on October 20.Oct 30, 2024 (day 32)Clinically stable without respiratory symptoms; CT showed partial resolution.Outpatient follow-up.Dec 3, 2024 (day 66) and Feb 20, 2025 (day 145)Serial CT showed continued absorption and progressive radiological improvement.Long-term standardized follow-up later became unavailable after family relocation. 2.Case presentationA 4-month-and-10-day-old boy was admitted on September 24 with a 2-day history of cough and fever and a 1-day history of diarrhea. Initially, he developed a paroxysmal cough with audible sputum in the throat and wheezing, without dyspnea or cyanosis. His maximum body temperature was 38.9 °C. One day before admission, he developed yellow watery stools 5–6 times per day. Symptomatic treatment, including anti-infective therapy, nebulization, and antidiarrheal therapy, did not relieve his symptoms.He was born at 32 + 6 weeks of gestation by cesarean section because of premature rupture of membranes, with a birth weight of 2.05 kg. His recent medical history was notable for hospitalization from September 20 to September 24, 2024, for adhesive intestinal obstruction, which improved after conservative treatment. There was no history of drug or food allergy. Although aspiration-related history was actively investigated at admission, the caregivers initially did not report any relevant oily substance exposure or choking episodes.On admission, his temperature was 37.8 °C, heart rate was 128 beats/min, respiratory rate was 32 breaths/min, oxygen saturation was 96%, and body weight was 5.2 kg. He was alert and responsive. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds bilaterally, with a few fine, moist rales and wheezes at the lung bases. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable except for the liver being palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin.Initial laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 18.11 × 109/L, hemoglobin of 101 g/L, platelet count of 475 × 109/L, C-reactive protein of 65.54 mg/L, and procalcitonin of 0.28 ng/mL. Stool viral testing was weakly positive for norovirus, whereas stool routine examination was normal. Chest radiography on September 24 showed patchy bilateral pulmonary opacities. Throat-swab targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) detected Klebsiella aerogenes.The patient was initially diagnosed with bronchopneumonia and norovirus enteritis and was treated with nasal cannula oxygen, empirical antimicrobial therapy, nebulization, and supportive care. On September 28, his condition deteriorated, with tachypnea, labored breathing, and inspiratory retractions, and he was transferred to the PICU. Repeat testing showed a procalcitonin level of 0.22 ng/mL and a BNP level of 112.70 pg/mL. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral patchy and confluent consolidations with surrounding ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and a crazy-paving pattern (Figures 1A–C). A focal area of fat attenuation (−30 to −150 HU) was identified within a right lung consolidation (Figures 2A,C). Because no relevant oily substance exposure history was available at that time, this finding was not initially recognized as suggestive of ELP.Figure 1Representative axial lung-window chest CT images obtained at PICU admission. (A–C) Bilateral patchy and confluent consolidations with surrounding ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and crazy-paving changes are shown at three thoracic levels.Panel A shows an axial chest CT scan with patchy areas of increased opacity in one lung. Panel B and panel C, both axial chest CT scans, display widespread bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation.Figure 2Representative paired chest CT images obtained at PICU admission. (A,C) Mediastinal-window images showing focal areas of fat attenuation within the right lung consolidation, with representative ROI attenuation values of −80 HU and −141 HU, respectively. (B,D) Corresponding lung-window images at the same anatomical levels, showing bilateral patchy and confluent consolidations with surrounding ground-glass opacities and interlobular septal thickening.Panel A displays a chest CT scan cross-section with a red circle and annotation showing –80 HU within the right lower lung. Panel B shows the same CT slice with higher contrast, emphasizing lung parenchyma texture. Panel C presents another CT cross-section with a red circle and annotation showing –141 HU, also in the right lower lung. The morphology was compatible with lipid-containing material but was not diagnostic because lipid-specific staining was unavailable.Microscopy comparison of two stained tissue samples labeled A and B, each showing numerous purple-stained cells on a light background. BALF tNGS also detected K. aerogenes, and sputum culture yielded the same organism. Meropenem was therefore continued as susceptibility-concordant antimicrobial therapy.On September 30, persistent fever, cough, tachypnea, and radiological progression prompted repeated targeted history-taking, and ELP was first suspected. The caregivers then disclosed that, during the previous hospitalization for adhesive intestinal obstruction, liquid paraffin had been administered orally multiple times by the caregivers using a spoon while the infant was held upright. The exact dose per administration and total number of administrations could not be reliably reconstructed from the available records and caregiver recall. Brief coughing and choking occurred only during administration; the caregivers regarded these episodes as transient difficulty with oral medication and did not report them to the medical team. Consequently, no targeted aspiration precautions or formal swallowing assessment were initiated at that time. Evidence supporting IVIG is limited to observational experience, and its independent contribution cannot be determined because bronchoalveolar lavage, corticosteroids, antimicrobial therapy, respiratory support, postural drainage, and IVIG were administered concurrently (21–23).Available follow-up through day 145 showed progressive radiological improvement. However, standardized pulmonary function testing, exercise-tolerance assessment, and imaging beyond day 145 were unavailable after the family relocated to another province. Therefore, residual interstitial abnormalities, later fibrosis, or impaired pulmonary function cannot be completely excluded. Other limitations include the absence of lipid-specific staining and histopathological confirmation, the coexistence of infection and sterile inflammatory injury, and the inability to attribute recovery to any single intervention.In summary, ELP should be considered in infants with treatment-refractory pneumonia, particularly when CT demonstrates intralesional fat attenuation. Detailed and repeated exposure history-taking is essential. In this case, discontinuation of paraffin exposure and multimodal management were associated with clinical and radiological improvement; however, the efficacy of individual interventions, particularly IVIG, cannot be inferred from a single case, and continued long-term follow-up remains important.

full_text_excerpt: Diagnosis requires integration of exposure history, imaging, BALF findings, microbiological evidence, and clinical course. Infectious pneumonia was initially favored because of fever, leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, bilateral pulmonary opacities, and positive respiratory microbiological findings. Lesions are often bilateral and multifocal, with middle- and lower-lobe and dependent posterior predominance in aspiration-related cases; peripheral sparing is not a typical or specific finding (1, 15, 16). A solitary fat-attenuation focus is supportive but not independently diagnostic and should be interpreted with the exposure history and other findings.Several diagnostic limitations should be acknowledged. The diagnosis was therefore clinical, based on the combined exposure history, CT findings, BALF morphology, and clinical course (1, 17–19).Another important consideration was concomitant bacterial lower respiratory tract infection. The concordant microbiological findings, together with persistent fever, airway secretions, pulmonary moist rales, respiratory deterioration, and bilateral pulmonary opacities, supported clinically significant infection rather than incidental upper-airway colonization. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to highlight the importance of recognizing exogenous lipoid pneumonia in infants with treatment-refractory pneumonia and intralesional fat attenuation on CT. The background emphasizes that ELP is a rare noninfectious inflammatory lung disease caused by aspiration or inhalation of exogenous lipids, which can mimic infectious pneumonia.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a case report involving a 4-month-old former preterm infant admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with severe pneumonia. The patient had a history of repeated paraffin oil aspiration and was diagnosed with exogenous lipoid pneumonia complicated by a Klebsiella aerogenes lower respiratory tract infection.
analysis.methods: The methods included targeted history-taking, chest CT imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytology, and next-generation sequencing of throat-swab and BALF samples. Klebsiella aerogenes was detected through these assays, and the patient's clinical course was documented.
analysis.main_results: Repeated targeted history-taking revealed multiple oral administrations of liquid paraffin with choking episodes. Chest CT showed bilateral consolidation, ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, a crazy-paving pattern, and a focal area of fat attenuation. BALF cytology showed vacuolated histiocytes, although lipid-specific staining was unavailable. The patient showed clinical and radiological improvement following discontinuation of paraffin exposure and multimodal management.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The case emphasizes that coughing or choking during administration of an oily medication to an infant should prompt immediate discontinuation, assessment of aspiration risk, and notification of medical personnel. It also highlights the importance of integrating exposure history, imaging, BALF findings, microbiological evidence, and clinical course for diagnosis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the importance of detailed exposure history and early recognition of exogenous lipoid pneumonia in infants with treatment-refractory pneumonia and intralesional fat attenuation on CT. This can aid in timely intervention and improved patient outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the concurrent administration of several interventions and the incomplete long-term follow-up, which prevents determining the efficacy of individual treatments and late pulmonary outcomes. The evidence is moderate due to the case report nature and lack of controlled comparisons.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a rare pediatric case of exogenous lipoid pneumonia (ELP) caused by repeated paraffin oil aspiration in a 4-month-old former preterm infant. The patient presented with severe pneumonia, and despite initial antimicrobial therapy, ELP was suspected based on clinical and radiological progression. The case highlights the importance of detailed exposure history, early recognition, and timely intervention in diagnosing ELP. Key findings included bilateral consolidation, ground-glass opacities, and vacuolated histiocytes in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Klebsiella aerogenes was detected through targeted next-generation sequencing and sputum culture, indicating a concomitant lower respiratory tract infection. The patient showed clinical and radiological improvement after discontinuation of paraffin exposure and multimodal management. The study underscores the need for integrating exposure history, imaging, BALF findings, microbiological evidence, and clinical course for accurate diagnosis. However, the concurrent use of multiple interventions and incomplete follow-up limit the ability to assess individual treatment efficacy and long-term outcomes. The evidence is moderate due to the case report format and the absence of controlled studies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在强调在患有 治疗 难治性肺炎和 CT 病灶内脂肪衰减的婴儿中识别外源性类脂性肺炎的重要性。背景强调,ELP是一种罕见的非感染性炎症性肺部疾病,由误吸或吸入外源性脂质引起,可模仿感染性肺炎。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项 病例报告 项目,涉及一名 4 个月大的前早产儿,因严重肺炎入住儿科重症监护室。患者有反复石蜡油吸入史,诊断为外源性类脂性肺炎并发产气克雷伯菌下呼吸道感染。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括有针对性的病史采集、胸部 CT 成像、支气管肺泡灌洗液 (BALF) 细胞学检查以及咽拭子和 BALF 样本的新一代测序。通过这些检测检测到产气克雷伯氏菌,并记录了患者的临床病程。
elements_zh.main_results: 反复有针对性的病史采集显示,多次口服液体石蜡并伴有窒息事件。胸部 CT 显示双侧实变、毛玻璃样混浊、小叶间间隔增厚​​、疯狂铺路模式和局部脂肪衰减。BALF 细胞学显示空泡组织细胞,但无法进行脂质特异性染色。在停止石蜡暴露和多模式治疗后,患者表现出临床和放射学改善。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该案例强调,在给婴儿服用油性药物期间出现咳嗽或窒息,应立即停药,评估误吸风险,并通知医务人员。它还强调了整合暴露史、影像学、BALF 结果、微生物证据和 诊断 临床病程的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以告知患有 治疗 难治性肺炎和 CT 病灶内脂肪衰减的婴儿的详细暴露史和早期识别外源性类脂性肺炎的重要性。这有助于及时干预并改善患者的治疗结果。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到多种干预措施同时实施和不完整的长期随访的限制,这阻碍了确定个体 治疗 的疗效和晚期肺部结局。由于 病例报告 的性质和缺乏受控比较,证据是中等的。

full_text: This study provides the first comprehensive description of the clinical phenotype and outcomes of all known patients with the heterozygous IRF4 p.T95R variant. Stojcic et al. analyze 10 affected individuals, identifying shared clinical features, treatment responses, and outcomes, and consider implications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. IRF4 is a transcription factor within the interferon regulatory factor family that controls key aspects of lymphocyte differentiation and adaptive immunity. The heterozygous IRF4 p.Thr95Arg (p.T95R) variant affecting the DNA-binding domain was recently identified to cause a new inborn error of immunity, but the longitudinal clinical course and therapeutic implications remain incompletely defined. We performed detailed clinical characterization and follow-up of all 10 known patients. Each presented with early-onset combined immunodeficiency characterized by hypo- or agammaglobulinemia and marked susceptibility to opportunistic infections. Pulmonary disease was universal, and gastrointestinal involvement was associated with a more severe clinical course. Four patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; two survived, and two died. Notably, both deaths occurred in patients transplanted in the setting of active infection. These findings define IRF4 p.T95R as a profound combined immunodeficiency with high infectious burden and demonstrate that disease severity and intervention timing may contribute to transplant outcomes, supporting early diagnosis and timely transplantation before uncontrolled infection. Graphical Abstract A diagram illustrating the clinical phenotype of IRF4 T95R and its outcomes.The diagram is divided into three main sections. The top section describes the clinical features associated with IRF4 T95R. It includes icons and text labels indicating conditions such as hypo- or agamma globulinemia, combined immunodeficiency, age of onset less than 1 year, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, gastrointestinal manifestations, herpesviridae infections, and onychomycosis. The middle section shows the distribution of patients who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and those who did not. The bottom section outlines the outcomes of HSCT, including graft loss, death, good outcome, and active infection at HSCT. Each patient's timeline is divided into sections with specific medical conditions, treatments, and outcomes. Family 1, Patient 1. Family 2, Patient 2. Family 3, Patient 3. Family 4, Patient 4. Each family shows a chronological sequence of medical events, treatments, and outcomes for each patient. The timelines include details such as the use of antibiotics, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and other medications, as well as the timing of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Key events are marked with specific dates and descriptions, including the use of treatments like prednisone, rituximab, and tacrolimus. The timelines also highlight the occurrence of infections, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), and other complications. The use of different colors and markers helps to distinguish between respiratory, gastrointestinal, treatment, and transplant-associated events.Transplant approaches were heterogeneous, reflecting disease severity and donor availability, as well as varied local protocols. For their initial HSCT, two patients received matched unrelated donor grafts, and two underwent haploidentical related donor transplantation. One haploidentical recipient received an ex vivo TCRα/β- and CD19-depleted graft, while the other received posttransplant cyclophosphamide–based GVHD prophylaxis. Upfront conditioning regimens were primarily reduced-toxicity conditioning (RTC, 3/4), with myeloablative conditioning (MAC) in P4 (Table 2). 2/4 patients treated with RTC received treosulfan/fludarabine-based conditioning (Treo/Flu), whereas the remaining patient received a combination of treosulfan and busulfan. Salvage regimens were used in P2 following graft failure, including both RTC with Treo/Flu and reduced intensity conditioning with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and total body irradiation.Engraftment kinetics were generally prompt in successful procedures, with a median time to neutrophil recovery of 13 days (range 10–25 days) and platelet recovery a median of 14 days (range 11–20 days) for the first HSCT. Although donor chimerism exceeding 95% was achieved in all transplanted patients, durable engraftment was not consistently maintained. Primary graft failure or graft loss occurred in two of four patients. P2 required multiple subsequent transplants due to recurrent graft failure, including secondary graft loss in the setting of refractory CMV infection. Bone marrow aspirate following his second HSCT was edematous and necrotic without evidence of significant hematopoietic regeneration, demonstrating that damage to the hematopoietic niche may have contributed to his repeat graft failure. P4 experienced graft loss after the first HSCT and was awaiting re-transplantation at the time of writing. These findings highlight intrinsic challenges in achieving durable engraftment in this disorder.GVHD occurred in all transplanted patients despite prophylaxis. Acute GVHD was universal and frequently involved the skin and GI tract, with additional liver involvement. Severe manifestations included stage 4 lower GI GVHD and multi-organ involvement. One patient developed chronic GVHD with cutaneous depigmentation consistent with vitiligo (23). GVHD-directed therapies were intensive and multimodal (Table 2).Infectious complications were frequent and clinically consequential. Both patients who ultimately died had active infections at the time of HSCT: CMV in one (P2) and Cryptosporidium and norovirus in the other (P3). CMV reactivation and drug-resistant CMV disease contributed to graft failure and required CMV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte therapy in P2. Additional complications in those undergoing HSCT included BK virus–associated hemorrhagic cystitis, bacteremia, fungemia, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, and multidrug-resistant septicemia.All deaths in this cohort occurred following HSCT and were attributed to active infections at the time of transplant. Collectively, HSCT in four IRF4T95R patients was associated with high rates of graft instability, universal acute GVHD, and substantial infection-related morbidity and mortality. While immune reconstitution was achievable in selected patients, transplant-related toxicity remained a major determinant of outcome. Materials and methodsAll study participants and/or their parents/guardians provided written informed consent for sequencing, data analysis, and publication of findings. Research study protocols were approved by local institutions, specifically the University of British Columbia Clinical Research Ethics Board (H15-00641 and H18-02853); Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile de France II, Paris, France (reference: 2015-01-05; 2015-01-05 MS2); the French Advisory Committee on Data Processing in Medical Research (Comité Consultatif sur le Traitement de l’information en matière de Recherche dans le domaine de la Santé, Paris, France; reference: 15.297bis); the Vanderbilt University Medical Center Human Research Protection Program (Institutional Review Board no.: 200412); the University of Ulm ethics board, Germany (application number 156/11); and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health.All patients were identified by clinical teams to carry the IRF4 p.Thr95Arg variant through next-generation sequencing (NM_002460.4(IRF4):c.284C>G (p.Thr95Arg), ClinVar variation ID: 2987365; accession: VCV002987365.3). Biochemical workup of P1 to P7 was completed previously (22). Comprehensive clinical reports were analyzed to track clinical characteristics associated with each case. Clinical diagnoses were performed according to local guidelines. Classification of conditioning regimens was performed according to the EMBT handbook (41). Bioinformatics analysis of previously reported IRF4 variants was performed with Franklin by Genoox (https://franklin.genoox.com).Case summariesFamily 1, P1P1 was initially reported by the IRF4 International Consortium, with a follow-up recently published by Wang et al. (22, 23). The published findings of this case are briefly summarized here.P1 was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents and tolerated all pediatric vaccines, including BCG. Symptom onset was pneumonia at 6 mo, followed by repeated upper respiratory tract infections from 6 mo to 3 years. From age 3–8 years, he continued to have severe recurrent pneumonias, as well as bronchiectasis. At 7 years old, hypogammaglobulinemia with reduced B cells was diagnosed. IgG replacement therapy and prophylactic antimicrobials successfully reduced the frequency of respiratory infections. GI manifestations began at age 3 years with chronic diarrhea and led to worsening abdominal pain from age 11 years onward that partially resolved with prednisone. At age 10 years, P1 developed a non-itchy maculopapular rash on his face, limbs, hands, and feet and tested positive for EBV in peripheral blood.The decision was made to move to HSCT due to the recurrent infections despite conventional therapies. P1 was grafted from a matched unrelated donor at age 13 years. Platelet and neutrophil recovery were achieved at 11 and 12 days after HSCT, respectively. 25 days after HSCT, steroid-refractory grade II acute cutaneous GVHD was diagnosed, which resolved with ruxolitinib. Late-onset hemorrhagic cystitis was attributed to polyomavirus BK. At 80 days after HSCT, P1 presented with thrombocytopenia, successfully treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and thrombopoietin. At 6 mo after HSCT, he presented with chronic cutaneous GVHD and began steroid therapy, with GVHD resolving within 2 mo, but vitiligo depigmentation gradually developing on the face, limbs, and trunk. IVIG replacement therapy was discontinued at 9 mo after HSCT following B cell recovery, and complete donor chimerism was sustained over the 1-year follow-up period. T, B, and NK cells normalized to age-appropriate reference ranges by 30 mo after HSCT. A protective antibody response to hepatitis B vaccination was achieved after HSCT. All immunosuppressants were discontinued by 32 mo after HSCT, except baricitinib, which replaced ruxolitinib at 28 mo after HSCT. As of the last report at 36 mo after HSCT, P1 continued on baricitinib and has remained free of infections and GVHD (23).Family 2, P2P2 was born to nonconsanguineous parents, healthy apart from a maternal history of rheumatoid arthritis. He tolerated all routine immunizations and was otherwise healthy until 11 mo of age, when he presented with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Rhinovirus/enterovirus infection, PJP, CMV viremia, and Escherichia coli ventilator-associated pneumonia ensued. Immunological assessment revealed agammaglobulinemia, low class-switched memory B cells, an undetectable response to vaccination, and reduced lymphocyte proliferation. After treatment of his infections, P2 was started on a regimen of IVIG, cotrimoxazole and valganciclovir prophylaxis. P2 then moved to HSCT due to the overall clinical picture of CID with multidrug-resistant CMV viremia. At 22 mo, he received his first HSCT from a matched unrelated donor, with GVHD prophylaxis of tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). He received his second graft at 31 mo, followed by a replicate infusion at 32 mo. Due to the inability to procure more transplants from the original donor, both were sourced from the haploidentical father with TCR α-β and CD19 depletion. HSCT was repeatedly complicated by graft loss due to ongoing multidrug-resistant CMV and CMV–end organ disease.Since our last report, P2 received his third HSCT at age 33 mo. Respiratory decompensation, SOS, and cutaneous and hepatic GVHD developed. He was treated with positive pressure ventilation, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery for an abscess of the right lower lung, and a chest tube. Microbiology was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus, and pathology showed chronic pneumonitis and bronchopneumonia of multifactorial etiology. Chest tube removal 1 mo later was complicated by pneumothorax. Further assessment revealed colonic grade 1 GVHD, possible lung GVHD, and bronchoscopy positive for CMV and rhinovirus/enterovirus. full_text_sections.results: ResultsIRF4T95R cohort overviewTo date, 10 individuals with the IRF4T95R variant (NM_002460.4(IRF4):c.284C>G (p.Thr95Arg), ClinVar variation ID: 2987365, accession: VCV002987365.3) have been identified. Seven were included in the original report (22), and patients are therefore numbered according to that initial publication. A follow-up clinical report for patient 1 (P1) was recently published by Wang and colleagues, and these results have been incorporated into the present analysis (23). Patients 8, 9, and 10 (P8, P9, and P10) are newly reported in this cohort, having been identified to carry the IRF4T95R variant by next-generation sequencing. P10 is also discussed by Vignesh et al. (unpublished data).Seven of 10 cases are formally documented to have arisen de novo. The mean age of surviving patients at last follow-up was 14 years (range 6.5–31 years; median 10.5 years) (Fig. 2 B). Of the four patients who received HSCT, two died: P2 at 3 years of age from multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and P3 at 12 years 10 mo of age from thrombotic microangiopathy-associated multi-organ failure. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis study expands current understanding of the disease course associated with the heterozygous IRF4T95R variant by defining the clinical manifestations and treatment outcomes in 10 affected patients, representing all diagnosed cases (22, 23). As such, this series provides the most comprehensive description currently available of this rare disorder.IRF4 T95R combined immunodeficiency is defined by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections. Patients are at particularly high risk of morbidity and mortality from opportunistic and viral pathogens, including P. jirovecii, EBV, CMV, and Cryptosporidium. Laboratory investigation demonstrated evidence of combined humoral and cellular immune dysfunction (22, 24) (Table S2). B cell immunity was profoundly impaired, with very low or absent serum antibody levels, reduced total CD19+ B cell numbers, and a marked differentiation arrest characterized by accumulation of naïve B cells and depletion of class-switched memory B cells and plasmablasts. T cell immunity was quantitatively preserved but qualitatively abnormal, with altered subset distribution, reduced Th17 and TFH populations, and impaired cytokine production, including reduced IL-2 and IFN-γ. Together, infection history and laboratory evidence of combined humoral and cellular immune dysfunction support IRF4T95R causing a profound combined immunodeficiency (CID).Clinically, patients exhibited early-onset, severe, and recurrent infections involving multiple organ systems. Respiratory disease was universal, with most patients developing pneumonia within the first year of life, frequently due to P. jirovecii. Additional respiratory complications included bronchiectasis and airway hyperreactivity, underscoring progressive pulmonary involvement as a defining feature. GI manifestations, a recognized component of many IEIs (25, 26), were observed in eight patients, commonly infection-associated. Notably, GI involvement was associated with an overall more severe clinical course, including progression to HSCT, whereas patients without GI disease had comparatively favorable outcomes. This interpretation is, however, limited by the small sample size and circular nature of causality, with it remaining undetermined if underlying GI dysfunction predisposed to infection, or if infection preceded GI dysfunction. It thus remains to be explored if GI dysfunction acts as an independent prognostic marker or simply a surrogate for uncontrolled infections. Finally, allergic inflammation was present in 20% of our cohort, consistent with the rate in the general population (27). Together, these findings establish IRF4T95R-associated disease as a CID with prominent respiratory involvement and variable but important GI disease.Of the 10 known IRF4T95R patients, only two are female (P6 and P9). Both generally exhibited a milder disease course, with neither experiencing any chronic infections, GI manifestations, or respiratory failure requiring ventilation. Ultimately, identification of additional patients will be required to determine whether biological sex modifies the clinical phenotype of IRF4 T95R.Management of IRF4T95R patients has largely relied on prevention and treatment of infection, including prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, fluconazole, and Ig replacement therapy. Although these measures reduce infection frequency, they do not fully prevent recurrent infections or disease-related complications. Given the severity and breadth of immune dysfunction observed in these patients, HSCT should be considered on an individual basis to optimize long-term outcomes. This rationale is supported by the tissue expression pattern of IRF4, which is highly enriched in hematopoietic lineages (28). HSCT thus has the potential to restore immune function and improve survival and quality of life when appropriately tailored to patient-specific factors. The primary triggers for moving to transplant in our cohort varied, primarily centering around frequency and severity of infections. However, the observation that two patients have survived into their third and fourth decades of life without HSCT underscores that supportive care alone can confer meaningful clinical benefit in selected cases. Even with the most up-to-date treatment, patients are at lifelong risk of opportunistic infections, which can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. This highlights the need for careful, individualized risk–benefit assessment when considering HSCT.HSCT in IRF4T95R-associated disease carries a substantial risk when performed in the setting of active infection. In our cohort, transplant-related mortality occurred exclusively in patients with uncontrolled infection at the time of HSCT, reinforcing the importance of timing as the most modifiable approach to improve outcomes. Successful engraftment resulted in immune reconstitution, supporting the curative potential of HSCT when undertaken before irreversible organ damage and infectious deterioration. Conditioning approaches varied by site according to patient status and local guidelines. Generally, patients who received Treo/Flu conditioning for their first graft (P2 and P3) had worse outcomes, including endothelial damage (SOS and thrombotic microangiopathy) and death, despite reduced-toxicity regimens (29). Due to our small cohort and the complex clinical status of these patients, it is not possible to determine if an alternative conditioning approach would be more suitable. While all deaths in this cohort occurred after transplant, these were the more severe cases pre-transplant, and thus those less likely to have good outcomes owing to their already fragile health status.A notable feature of this cohort is the high rates of both graft failure and GVHD. Two patients (P2 and P4) experienced graft failure following HSCT. P2 had secondary graft failure of his first graft and primary failure of his second. Engraftment was finally achieved following the fourth HSCT. In the case of P2, active CMV and the use of third-party anti-CMV cytotoxic T lymphocytes may have been a contributing factor (30). Before transplantation, P4 was treated for anti-donor antibodies and COVID-19, which may underlie P4’s graft failure despite busulfan-based MAC. Together, graft loss in our cohort may be attributable to a wide number of factors, including underlying infection and/or inflammatory status (31, 32).All transplanted patients were affected by GVHD, possibly influenced by pre-existing active inflammation and enteropathy at the time of transplant. We previously described upregulation of CXCL13 3–4.5 times that of healthy controls in this cohort (22). Elevated CXCL13 has been linked to GVHD in both murine models and human patients (33, 34). This may thus predispose this cohort to GVHD. Furthermore, elevated CXCL13 has also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease, showing a positive correlation with inflammation severity, further supported by CXCL13 knockout mice that demonstrated reduced colitis severity (35, 36). It is plausible that elevated CXCL13 could contribute indirectly to the apparent engraftment defect in our cohort. Other biomarkers, such as ferritin and type I and II IFNs, could provide further insight. In our cohort, ferritin was normal for all patients assessed, and type II IFNs were reduced; however, type I IFNs were not assessed (22). Further work may benefit from the analysis of a range of biomarkers in this patient population, particularly before and after transplant.To date, multiple distinct IEIs affecting IRF4 have been described, each characterized by different genetic lesions, inheritance patterns, and spectra of infectious susceptibility (7) (Fig. 4 and Table S4). Accordingly, IEIs involving IRF4 should be considered as discrete clinical and molecular entities rather than grouped under the imprecise and potentially misleading label of “IRF4 deficiency.”Figure 4. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHuman inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), which include primary immunodeficiencies, primary immune regulatory disorders, and primary atopic disorders, encompass a broad group of genetic disorders impairing immune function (1, 2, 3, 4). The phenotypes of the over 550 known IEIs span immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, autoinflammation, allergy, and malignancy (5). Tracking the clinical outcomes of these rare diseases not only informs patient diagnosis and management but also expands our understanding of fundamental human biology.Interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) are a group of nine transcription factors initially identified to play a crucial role in promoting type I interferon (IFN) production (6, 7). IRFs are transiently upregulated during antimicrobial responses, where they primarily act as transcriptional mediators in IFN-induced signaling pathways (8). Beyond IFN signaling, IRFs mediate a range of immune processes, including cytokine production and the differentiation, development, and function of lymphoid and myeloid cells (9, 10, 11, 12, 13). IRF6 is unique in that it primarily mediates epithelial function and craniofacial development rather than immune responses (7, 14, 15).IRF4, also known as MUM1, Pip, LSRIF, and ICSAT, has a vital role in immune function; however, unlike the majority of other IRFs, its primary role is not mediating IFN signaling. Instead, IRF4 is predominantly expressed in T and B cells, where it is crucial for lymphocyte development (16, 17). Multiple B cell functions rely on IRF4, including differentiation, activation, receptor editing, proliferation, class switch recombination, and plasma cell formation (9, 18, 19). Mice deficient in Irf4 exhibit impaired late-stage B cell maturation and markedly reduced serum Ig levels (9). Irf4 also plays a critical role in T cell biology, with T cell differentiation and effector fate decisions governed by graded Irf4 expression downstream of TCR signal strength (20, 21).In 2023, the IRF4 International Consortium defined a novel IEI caused by a recurrent heterozygous missense variant affecting the DNA-binding domain of IRF4 (IRF4 NM_001195286.2 c.284C>G, p.Thr95Arg, henceforth IRF4T95R) (Fig. 1 A), identified in seven patients from six unrelated kindreds (22). IRF4T95R patients presented with fully penetrant, early-onset, autosomal dominant combined immunodeficiency. Key clinical features included marked susceptibility to opportunistic infections, most notably Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). In addition, patients experienced significant viral infections, including CMV and EBV, as well as mycobacterial infections. Patients had reduced CD19+ B cells with a prominent maturation defect, with increased naïve and transitional B cells, defective plasma cell differentiation, reduced class-switched memory B cells, and agammaglobulinemia. Furthermore, T helper 17 (Th17) and T follicular helper (TFH) cells were reduced with impaired IL-12 and IFN-γ production, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were distributed abnormally in the multidimensional space. Three are found in the DNA-binding domain, including IRF4 p.T95R, and two are located in the IRF association domain. (B) IRF4 p.T95R demonstrates unusual multimorphic effects: hypermorphic through increased DNA-binding affinity, hypomorphic with poor expression of canonical IRF4 target genes, and neomorphic with expression of non-canonical targets such as CXCL13. Panel B illustrates the multimorphic effects of the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including loss of function, gain of function, and new function, with specific impacts on gene binding and expression.Biochemically, IRF4T95R protein levels were normal in multiple cell types, but B cells transduced with IRF4T95R demonstrated abnormal IRF4 localization, impaired class switch recombination, and reduced plasma cell differentiation. DNA-binding affinity was increased, likely due to the change to positively charged arginine, allowing more and longer interactions with DNA, resulting in an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. title_original: IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency: Clinical features and transplant outcomes

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to characterize the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare disorder associated with severe susceptibility to infections. The background highlights the need to understand the disease course and treatment outcomes in affected individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 10 patients with the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including four who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Patients spanned four continents, with disease onset uniformly early (<1 year) and a male predominance (8/10).
analysis.methods: Patients received HSCT with varying donor sources, conditioning regimens, and immunosuppression protocols. One patient had multiple HSCT donors, with the initial graft from a matched unrelated donor and subsequent grafts from the same mismatched related donor. Outcomes were evaluated based on survival and complications following transplant.
analysis.main_results: Two patients survived with a median follow-up of 37 months, while two died at 9 and 12.5 months post-HSCT. One death was due to multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and another was from thrombotic microangiopathy-associated multi-organ failure. Both patients had active infections (CMV and Cryptosporidium) at the time of transplant.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency is characterized by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections, with HSCT outcomes being mixed. This study provides the most comprehensive description of the disorder to date.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the management of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, particularly regarding the risks and outcomes of HSCT in the context of active infections. They also highlight the importance of early diagnosis and tailored immunosuppression strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective nature and the small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of prospective data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare genetic disorder causing severe susceptibility to infections. Four of the 10 patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with mixed results: two survived, while two died from complications related to active infections at the time of transplant. The authors interpret that this condition is marked by broad immune dysfunction, with HSCT outcomes influenced by the presence of concurrent infections. The findings contribute to understanding the disease course and treatment challenges, emphasizing the need for careful management of infections in affected individuals. However, the study's retrospective design and small sample size limit the strength of the evidence, suggesting a moderate confidence level in the conclusions.

elements_zh.methods: 患者接受不同供体来源、预处理方案和免疫抑制方案的 HSCT。一名患者有多个 HSCT 供体,最初的移植物来自匹配的无关供体,随后的移植物来自同一不匹配的相关供体。根据移植后的存活率和并发症评估结果。
elements_zh.main_results: 两名患者在中位随访 37 个月后存活,两名患者在 HSCT 后 9 个月和 12.5 个月死亡。一名死亡是由于多重耐药肺炎克雷伯菌感染,另一名死亡是由于血栓性微血管病相关的多器官衰竭。两名患者在移植时均存在活动性感染(CMV 和隐孢子虫)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,IRF4 p.T95R 联合免疫缺陷的特点是对广谱感染具有明显的易感性,而 HSCT 的结果则参差不齐。这项研究提供了迄今为止对该疾病最全面的描述。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 IRF4 p.T95R 联合免疫缺陷患者的管理提供了信息,特别是关于活动性感染情况下 HSCT 的风险和结果。他们还强调了早期 诊断 和定制免疫抑制策略的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性和样本量小而受到限制,这可能会影响结果的普遍性。由于缺乏前瞻性数据并且可能存在未测量的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to characterize the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare disorder associated with severe susceptibility to infections. The background highlights the need to understand the disease course and treatment outcomes in affected individuals.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 10 patients with the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including four who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Patients spanned four continents, with disease onset uniformly early (<1 year) and a male predominance (8/10).
analysis_en.methods: Patients received HSCT with varying donor sources, conditioning regimens, and immunosuppression protocols. One patient had multiple HSCT donors, with the initial graft from a matched unrelated donor and subsequent grafts from the same mismatched related donor. Outcomes were evaluated based on survival and complications following transplant.
analysis_en.main_results: Two patients survived with a median follow-up of 37 months, while two died at 9 and 12.5 months post-HSCT. One death was due to multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and another was from thrombotic microangiopathy-associated multi-organ failure. Both patients had active infections (CMV and Cryptosporidium) at the time of transplant.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency is characterized by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections, with HSCT outcomes being mixed. This study provides the most comprehensive description of the disorder to date.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the management of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, particularly regarding the risks and outcomes of HSCT in the context of active infections. They also highlight the importance of early diagnosis and tailored immunosuppression strategies.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective nature and the small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of prospective data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors.

title_zh: IRF4 p.T95R 联合免疫缺陷:临床特征和移植结果
source_body_en: This study provides the first comprehensive description of the clinical phenotype and outcomes of all known patients with the heterozygous IRF4 p.T95R variant. These findings define IRF4 p.T95R as a profound combined immunodeficiency with high infectious burden and demonstrate that disease severity and intervention timing may contribute to transplant outcomes, supporting early diagnosis and timely transplantation before uncontrolled infection. Conditioning methods include reduced-toxicity conditioning for three patients and myeloablative conditioning for one patient.
